studies.headline: Breathing thin air shifts the body clock — but not as well as morning light
studies.summary: In a randomised crossover study, 11 healthy adults (mean age 23.3 years) were exposed to normobaric hypoxia (12% oxygen for 2 hours, equivalent to high-altitude air) and compared to a combined luminotherapy-plus-melatonin condition, both designed to simulate a 4-hour circadian phase advance. Circadian phase was measured via salivary dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO). Light-and-melatonin produced a statistically significant phase advance of ~78 minutes, while hypoxia produced an average advance of ~35 minutes that did not reach statistical significance.
studies.why_it_matters: Jet lag, shift work and sleep disorders affect millions of people, and the search for new tools to reset the body clock is active; this exploratory study is among the first to test low-oxygen exposure as a circadian intervention in humans, opening a novel avenue for research even if the effect was modest and inconclusive.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), short follow-up, single-center. Only 11 participants, all young healthy adults; the hypoxia effect did not reach statistical significance; results are explicitly exploratory and the authors caution that no conclusions can yet be drawn about whether hypoxia truly causes circadian shifts *Editor's fact-check note: The hypoxia phase advance of ~35 min was explicitly described as not statistically significant in the abstract; this is accurately reflected in the summary. N=11 confirmed from abstract.*

studies.headline: What you expect your symptoms to do matters more than how doctors frame them
studies.summary: Researchers enrolled 217 patients with somatic symptom disorder in a 10-day smartphone-based study, randomly assigning them to receive daily prompts framing their symptoms either as causing impairment or as allowing freedom from impairment. Symptom severity and symptom expectations both declined slightly over the 10 days, and the two tracked each other closely. Crucially, patients who started the study with lower symptom expectations improved faster — but the framing manipulation itself produced no significant effect, suggesting that simply reframing how patients think about symptoms in the short term does not move the needle.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that a patient's pre-existing symptom expectations may be a more powerful driver of symptom course than brief framing interventions, pointing researchers toward the need for deeper or longer-lasting strategies for changing those expectations.
studies.caveats: short follow-up, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Only 10 days of follow-up; longer reframing interventions may yet prove effective. Outcomes were self-reported via smartphone. Conducted at a single German university medical centre, so generalisability is uncertain *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=217, 10-day EMA design, randomized framing groups, null result for framing, and significant association between baseline expectations and rate of symptom decline. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: Toddlers almost never see emotional faces — and when they do, it's nearly always happiness
studies.summary: Researchers fitted 26 toddler–caregiver pairs with head-mounted cameras to capture each person's egocentric (first-person) view during everyday home activities, then used automated computer vision to quantify how often faces and emotional expressions appeared in each perspective. Faces were sparse in toddlers' views and significantly less frequent than in caregivers' views. Across both perspectives, happiness dominated; negative expressions were extremely rare, and expressions appeared in clusters rather than steadily. Notably, toddlers encountered surprised faces relatively often, while caregivers saw more happy and sad faces than their children did.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding challenges the assumption that young children are immersed in rich streams of emotional facial signals, suggesting that toddlers learn to read faces from surprisingly limited — and positivity-skewed — input, which could reshape theories of emotional and social development.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center. Very small sample of 26 families; automated computer-vision coding may miss nuanced or partial expressions; all families were studied at home in the UK, which may not represent all caregiving cultures *Editor's fact-check note: N=26 families confirmed from abstract. Computer vision models used for annotation — automated, not human-coded — noted as a methodological nuance but not a standard caveat flag; no correction needed.*

studies.headline: One in five clozapine prescriptions worldwide is for a condition other than schizophrenia
studies.summary: Researchers analysed clozapine prescribing data from 55 countries across 15 regions using the IQVIA MIDAS Disease Insights database, drawing on electronic medical records, prescription/claims data, and patient medication records. Although clozapine is formally approved primarily for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, the study found that approximately 18% of all recorded prescribing indications fell outside schizophrenia spectrum disorders — including mood disorders (13.6%), anxiety disorders (2.5%), and movement disorders (1.1%). Regional variation was substantial: in African and Asian regions, off-label use accounted for an average of 34.3% and 21% of recorded indications respectively, compared with much lower rates elsewhere.
studies.why_it_matters: Clozapine carries serious side-effect risks including potentially fatal agranulocytosis, so widespread off-label use without international evidence-based guidance raises real questions about patient safety and prescribing rationale across different health systems.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, self-reported outcomes (prescribing indication data may be incomplete or inconsistently recorded across regions), industry funding (IQVIA database used; some authors report honoraria from multiple pharmaceutical companies). Data come from a commercial database (IQVIA) which may not capture all prescribing, and recording of indications varies in completeness across countries; the study is descriptive and cannot establish whether off-label use is clinically appropriate or harmful; several authors have financial ties to pharmaceutical companies *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract does not report a total N of individual patients — it reports prescribing indication data aggregated across 55 countries/15 regions from a commercial database. Summary and caveats reflect this accurately. 'Industry funding' flag applied because the data source is a commercial IQVIA product and several authors declared pharmaceutical company honoraria, though no direct study funding source is stated in the abstract.*

studies.headline: Mindfulness is linked to better mental health in Black mothers facing discrimination — but it doesn't buffer the harm
studies.journal: Cultural Diversity and Ethnic Minority Psychology
studies.summary: Researchers analysed cross-sectional survey data from 305 Black American mothers (average age 37) to examine how discrimination experiences related to anxiety, depressive symptoms, and psychological wellbeing, and whether mindfulness or meditation frequency changed that relationship. Discrimination was associated with worse mental health across all three outcomes. Mindfulness and meditation were independently linked to lower anxiety and better wellbeing — but neither moderated (i.e., buffered) the negative effects of discrimination. The counterintuitive finding is that mindfulness compensates for rather than protects against discrimination's harms.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests mindfulness may help Black mothers maintain psychological wellbeing under discrimination, but does not reduce discrimination's direct toll — a distinction with real implications for how mental health support is framed and offered to this group.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, cross-sectional (2015 data), single-country (US). Cross-sectional data collected in 2015 cannot establish causality; all measures are self-reported; sample is US-specific and may not generalise *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract explicitly states 'no significant moderating effects' — meaning mindfulness compensates additively but does not buffer discrimination. Summary and headline corrected to reflect this nuance clearly.*

studies.headline: Emotional volatility — not just mood — links impulsivity to drinking and risky sex in gay and bisexual men
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a secondary analysis of experience-sampling data from 248 moderate-to-heavy drinking sexual minority men, collected over two 3-week bursts, to examine whether emotional dynamics explain links between impulsivity and risky behaviour. Men with higher negative urgency (acting rashly when upset) showed greater variability and reactivity in negative affect, and this emotional volatility — not emotional inertia or average mood — was associated with heavier drinking and condomless anal intercourse in the following burst. Positive urgency was linked to positive affect reactivity but did not significantly predict risky behaviour indirectly.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding shifts focus from average emotional state to emotional instability as a key mechanism connecting impulsivity to substance use and sexual risk, suggesting interventions targeting mood regulation skills in volatile emotional moments may be more effective than those addressing general negative mood.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per subgroup analysis), observational design, self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis, single demographic group limiting generalisability. Secondary analysis; participants were moderate-to-heavy drinkers in a specific demographic (sexual minority men), limiting generalisability; self-reported outcomes; observational design precludes causal conclusions *Editor's fact-check note: N=248 overall exceeds N<100 threshold for the full sample, but 'small sample' flag retained because this is a secondary analysis of a specific demographic subgroup (sexual minority men); design is experience sampling, not a clinical trial.*

studies.summary: Researchers tested 127 participants in Brussels on their ability to recognise subtle, early-stage dynamic facial expressions of happiness, fear, and anger, while also measuring their metacognitive confidence in those judgements and their level of sensory processing sensitivity (SPS). studies.headline: Brain 'fingerprints' may one day flag suicide risk before it's visible to clinicians
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a narrative review of neuroimaging studies examining the brain connectivity patterns — the 'connectome' — associated with suicidal thoughts and behaviours. Drawing on MRI, PET, and EEG/MEG findings, they found convergent evidence that suicidality is associated with disrupted prefrontal-limbic-subcortical circuitry and reduced global network integration. The review also highlights emerging machine-learning approaches that use individualized connectome 'fingerprints' to model personal suicide risk, and proposes a novel normative-modelling framework for a connectome-based suicide risk calculator.
studies.why_it_matters: Suicide claims over 700,000 lives globally each year, and objective biological tools for risk assessment remain elusive; this review suggests that brain-connectivity profiling could one day complement clinical assessment, though validation in large longitudinal cohorts is still needed.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, single-center (primary authors China-based), short follow-up in underlying studies. This is a narrative review, not a clinical tool — no risk calculator yet exists. Underlying studies are largely observational and single-centre (predominantly China). Longitudinal validation in diverse populations has not yet been done. Journalists should avoid implying this is ready for clinical use *Editor's fact-check note: This is a review article, not a primary empirical study with a defined N. The summary has been written to reflect its review/synthesis nature rather than implying a single participant sample. No N is stated in the abstract, which is consistent with a narrative review.*

studies.headline: Tracking alcohol recovery daily doesn't change how people actually behave
studies.summary: Researchers randomly assigned 192 adults engaged with Alcoholics Anonymous to either complete twice-daily ecological momentary assessment (EMA) surveys for 6 months or a minimal assessment condition with only three assessments over the same period. Across 240 statistical comparisons, only 8 differences were significant — consistent with chance — and no meaningful group differences emerged for days abstinent, AA attendance, or drinks per drinking day. The findings suggest that intensive, repeated self-monitoring does not systematically alter the very behaviors it is measuring, addressing a key concern in addiction research methodology.
studies.why_it_matters: EMA is increasingly used in addiction research; this study suggests researchers can trust that frequent check-ins are not artificially inflating or deflating the recovery behaviors they aim to study.
studies.caveats: single-center, self-reported outcomes. Single site (University of New Mexico), self-reported outcomes, findings specific to AA context and may not generalise to other recovery programmes or addictions

studies.headline: Economic chaos in the 1990s still shapes Eastern European men's working lives three decades on
studies.summary: Swedish researchers used retrospective data from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE; N=10,999) across 11 Central and Eastern European countries to track how hardship during the post-socialist transition (1987–93) shaped work trajectories over 31 years. Among men, both prolonged employment gaps and financial hardship during that period were associated with elevated risk of later unemployment, while experiencing significant stress increased the risk of health-related withdrawal from the labour market. Women showed fewer significant effects, with extended employment gaps being the strongest predictor of later unemployment.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that economic crises leave lasting imprints on individuals' working lives — particularly for men — even decades later, with implications for how policymakers design safety nets during periods of major economic disruption.
studies.caveats: observational design, retrospective self-reported data, region-specific (Central and Eastern Europe). Retrospective self-reported data on events 30+ years ago introduces recall bias; observational design cannot prove causation; findings specific to post-socialist Central and Eastern Europe

studies.headline: Latinx infants hear more songs sung directly to them than other US babies do
studies.summary: Researchers used daylong audio recordings (LENA devices) and crowdsourced annotation by 417 listeners to characterise the auditory home environments of 64 Latinx US infants aged 4–23 months, then compared results to a previously published non-Latinx US sample. However, unlike non-Latinx infants—who heard more non-infant-directed music—Latinx infants heard more infant-directed (ID) music, i.e., songs and singing addressed specifically to them, and received greater overall music exposure. The study suggests enhanced ID music exposure in Latinx homes may support multiple developmental domains.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes not applicable — but bootstrapping comparison to prior dataset rather than direct matched comparison is a methodological limitation. studies.headline: Novelty-seeking personality predicts faster depression relief — but the effect may be a placebo artefact

The finding did not survive correction for multiple comparisons and is therefore considered preliminary.

studies.headline: LGBTQ+ people in Rwanda experience legal ambiguity as an everyday physical reality, not just a policy gap
studies.summary: Researchers at Rwanda's Health Development Initiative used in-depth interviews, focus groups, and digital storytelling with 57 LGBTQ+ participants across six Rwandan districts to explore their lived experiences. Thematic analysis identified five levels of experience — individual, interpersonal, community, organisational, and policy — shaped by internalised stigma, family rejection, healthcare discrimination, and employment barriers. A key finding was that legal ambiguity (Rwanda neither criminalises nor protects LGBTQ+ identities) is not experienced as neutral but as an embodied, daily negotiation of hostile spaces. Community organisations emerged as important sources of resilience.
studies.why_it_matters: The study illustrates that the absence of explicit criminalisation does not equate to safety or belonging, with implications for how global health and human rights organisations assess LGBTQ+ vulnerability in legally ambiguous contexts.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), qualitative/self-reported outcomes, single-country (Rwanda), purposive and snowball sampling. Small sample of 57 recruited via snowball sampling, which may over-represent more connected or activist community members; qualitative findings are not statistically generalisable; Rwanda-specific political and cultural context limits direct global application

studies.headline: Brain wave patterns in early-onset Alzheimer's are more chaotic than expected — and could aid diagnosis
studies.summary: Researchers compared resting-state gamma-frequency brain activity (30–48 Hz) and grey matter volumes in 24 early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD) patients confirmed by CSF biomarkers and 24 matched healthy controls. Rather than a uniform reduction in gamma activity, EOAD patients showed increased gamma power but regionally variable connectivity — some areas more connected, others less. A combined model of parietal gamma power and coherence achieved 83.3% classification accuracy (cross-validated: 77.1%; AUC = 0.844) in distinguishing patients from controls.
studies.why_it_matters: Early-onset Alzheimer's is notoriously difficult to detect before significant neurodegeneration occurs; if replicated in larger samples, gamma EEG signatures could offer a relatively low-cost, non-invasive diagnostic marker worth investigating further.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center. Only 24 patients and 24 controls, all from a single Turkish centre; results need replication in a much larger and more diverse cohort before any clinical application is conceivable

studies.headline: A nasal spray stops severe seizures in nearly two-thirds of out-of-hospital emergencies
studies.summary: Researchers pooled data from two clinical studies to assess how well diazepam nasal spray worked when administered outside hospital settings for tonic-clonic status epilepticus — prolonged, dangerous seizures. Across 402 classified seizure episodes in patients aged 2–65 years, 61.7% of episodes terminated within 30 minutes of seizure onset, and nearly half (49.8%) stopped within 20 minutes of receiving the spray. Recurrence within 24 hours was low (under 5%), and fewer than 6% of episodes required a second dose, suggesting the single-dose treatment was broadly effective.
studies.why_it_matters: Status epilepticus is a life-threatening emergency, and most seizures occur outside hospital settings; evidence that a nasal spray can terminate the majority of prolonged seizures at home or in the community could inform emergency care guidelines and caregiver training.
studies.caveats: observational design, retrospective analysis, industry funding [Neurelis], secondary analysis. Retrospective pooled analysis, not a randomised controlled trial; multiple authors employed by or formerly employed by Neurelis, the drug's manufacturer; serious treatment-related events occurred in 6.6% of patients with status epilepticus episodes *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states serious treatment-emergent events of SE occurred in 6.6% of patients — this is a safety caveat not reflected in the original summary draft; added for accuracy. The study is a retrospective combined cohort analysis (secondary analysis of pooled phase 1/2a and phase 3 data), not a prospective RCT. Several authors are affiliated with Neurelis, the manufacturer of diazepam nasal spray (Valtoco), constituting industry funding/conflict of interest.*

studies.headline: Your DNA alone cannot predict how psychiatric drugs will work in your body, new review argues
studies.summary: This narrative review from researchers in Mexico re-examines the foundational assumption of psychiatric pharmacogenetics — that inherited variants in cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes reliably predict how patients metabolise and respond to psychotropic drugs. They conclude that metabolic capacity should be understood as a dynamic functional state rather than a fixed inherited trait, suggesting precision psychiatry needs to move beyond static genotyping.
studies.why_it_matters: Pharmacogenetic testing — where a patient's DNA is used to guide antidepressant or antipsychotic dosing — is rapidly expanding in clinical practice, so evidence that genotype alone may be an insufficient predictor has significant implications for how these tests are marketed and used.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center (review from one research group), no original human participant data (narrative review only). studies.headline: Anxiety fuels problem drinking and gambling mainly in people who avoid their own feelings

studies.headline: People who carry a fragile X gene variant show unusual brain activity when trying to control their emotions and thoughts
studies.summary: Researchers used functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure brain activity in 14 female carriers of the FMR1 premutation — a genetic variant linked to Fragile X syndrome — while they completed emotional inhibition and cognitive conflict tasks (Go/No-Go and Stroop). studies.why_it_matters: FMR1 premutation carriers — estimated at roughly 1 in 150 women — often experience executive and emotional difficulties that are poorly understood; this study suggests a specific brain-level signature that could eventually guide targeted support strategies.

studies.headline: A new caregiver-completed scale captures hidden struggles in Dravet syndrome that standard tools miss
studies.summary: Researchers developed and validated the D-DAND scale — a caregiver-administered interview specifically designed to capture the full range of developmental and behavioural challenges in Dravet syndrome (DS), a severe childhood-onset epilepsy. The scale was standardised with caregivers of 123 individuals with DS aged 3–41 years across centres in Italy and France; a subsample of 43 caregivers completed it twice to test reliability. Test-retest reliability was excellent (r ≈ .98 overall), and the scale detected Dravet-specific features that widely used generic tools — such as the Childhood Autism Rating Scale and Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales — failed to capture.
studies.why_it_matters: Dravet syndrome involves far more than seizures, including autism-like behaviours, sleep disturbances, and cognitive difficulties, yet no validated Dravet-specific measurement tool previously existed; having one could improve clinical trials, personalise care, and give caregivers a structured voice in assessments.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 for reliability subsample), single-center (two centers), observational design. Reliability subsample was small (N=43); study conducted at only two specialist centres in Italy and France, limiting generalisability; scale is new and not yet validated against long-term clinical outcomes *Editor's fact-check note: Full standardisation sample was N=123 (not below 100), but the test-retest reliability subsample was N=43, which is below 100 — both figures noted. studies.summary: Researchers conducted a bibliometric analysis of 687 publications in top-tier (Q1) addiction journals with first authors affiliated with Spanish institutions, spanning from journal inception to December 2025. Female first authorship rose from 35.3% in 1986–1995 to 54.7% in 2016–2025, crossing the 50% threshold. Regression analysis confirmed a significant positive temporal trend (OR=1.036 per year, p<0.001). The authors caution that unmeasured structural and cultural factors may underlie the pattern.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that gender parity — and even a female majority — in scientific first authorship is achievable in fields historically dominated by men, though the authors note that crossing a statistical threshold does not mean structural barriers have been eliminated.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (Spain), self-reported or database-derived gender classification, limited to Q1 journals only. Data are limited to Spanish institutions and Q1 journals, so findings may not generalise globally. The study measures first authorship only — senior/last authorship and leadership roles are not captured. Gender was likely inferred from names or records rather than self-identified, which introduces potential misclassification. Unmeasured structural factors acknowledged by authors *Editor's fact-check note: N=687 publications confirmed from abstract. Direction of effect (increase from 35.3% to 54.7%) confirmed. No errors requiring correction.*

studies.headline: Being left out of a game does not make you feel less in control of your actions, study finds
studies.summary: Researchers ran two pre-registered experiments plus a high-powered follow-up study to test whether social exclusion — induced using the online Cyberball ball-tossing game — reduces people's sense of agency, as measured by 'temporal binding' (how tightly people perceive the link between their actions and outcomes). Across all three studies, social exclusion reliably changed participants' explicit feelings of control, but produced no detectable effect on interval estimation of action-outcome timing. Bayesian analyses in the follow-up supported the null result, and the researchers also identified a methodological issue: interval estimates drifted systematically across experimental blocks regardless of condition.
studies.why_it_matters: Prior research had suggested that feeling socially excluded shrinks your sense of personal agency — a finding that had implications for understanding the psychological harms of ostracism — but these well-powered, pre-registered results suggest the effect may be much more limited or measurement-dependent than assumed.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, online administration. All experiments were conducted online, which may affect how strongly participants experience the exclusion; the abstract does not report total participant numbers for each study; temporal binding measured via interval estimation may itself be an imperfect proxy for felt agency *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report a total N for the combined studies; individual sample sizes are not specified in the abstract text. 'Self-reported outcomes' is noted because the interval estimation task is a subjective perceptual measure, and Cyberball manipulation checks relied on self-report. Online administration is flagged as a relevant caveat given known issues with online Cyberball validity.*

studies.headline: Calming yourself down after a political shock may actually make you less likely to act on it
studies.summary: Researchers tracked the emotions and political motivations of US adults across two major political shocks — the Brett Kavanaugh Supreme Court confirmation (initial N=430, 2018) and the Trump impeachments and acquittals (initial N=979, 2019–2021). Using an affective science framework, the team found that for both Democrats and Republicans, using cognitive reappraisal (reframing events to feel better) was associated with more positive emotion — which in turn predicted greater motivation for political action. However, for Democrats specifically, reappraisal was also more strongly associated with reduced negative emotion, and that reduction in negative emotion was linked to lower motivation to act — suggesting that emotion regulation may have differentially dampened Democrats' drive to respond.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that the very psychological tools people use to cope with distressing political events may, under some conditions, reduce their motivation to engage politically — a counterintuitive tension between emotional wellbeing and civic participation that has broad implications for how we think about mental health and democracy.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, US-specific political context, short follow-up (per study period), secondary analysis. Both studies are observational with self-reported emotions, so causation cannot be established. Findings are rooted in specific US political events and may not translate to other political contexts or countries. Sample attrition over the follow-up periods should be noted *Editor's fact-check note: Sample sizes confirmed from abstract: Study 1 initial N=430, Study 2 initial N=979. Design is observational/longitudinal survey, not experimental manipulation — causal language avoided accordingly. 'Short follow-up' flag adjusted: Study 2 ran November 2019–February 2021, which is relatively extended, but Study 1 was September–October 2018 (short). Both flagged as short follow-up per study. studies.headline: Lonely people don't know when to trust their own social judgements
studies.summary: Researchers used a vignette-based social decision-making task to examine whether loneliness is linked to differences in decision confidence and how well that confidence tracks actual difficulty. Across two independent general population samples (N=6,517), higher loneliness was associated with lower overall decision confidence and, crucially, a reduced ability to adjust confidence appropriately as decisions became harder. These effects held after controlling for depression and anxiety, suggesting the pattern reflects something specific to loneliness rather than general psychological distress.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests lonely people may struggle not because they make systematically biased social choices, but because they cannot reliably gauge when their social judgements are trustworthy — a potential mechanism for why loneliness tends to persist even when opportunities for connection exist.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center (Poland). Cross-sectional design means causality cannot be established; self-reported loneliness and confidence measures; sample drawn from Poland, which may limit generalisability

studies.headline: Feeling financially stressed at home pushes teenagers into the crosshairs of cyberbullying — even when their family income hasn't changed
studies.summary: Researchers tracked 2,407 Chinese adolescents (mean age 12.75 years, 50.23% girls) from seven schools across three time points over one year, using a random intercept cross-lagged model to examine whether perceived economic stress — rather than objective income — predicted cybervictimization. At the individual (within-person) level, higher perceived economic stress predicted greater cybervictimization over time, and being cybervictimised in turn damaged the quality of teacher-student relationships. The relationship between economic stress and cybervictimization was partly explained by the erosion of teacher-student relationships, which appeared to serve as a protective buffer. Notably, between-person differences in economic stress were not associated with cybervictimization, meaning it was changes within the same adolescent over time — not differences between richer and poorer students — that drove the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that subjective financial worry — not just poverty itself — may leave adolescents socially vulnerable, and that strengthening teacher-student relationships could be a practical way to reduce cyberbullying risk.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center (seven schools, one region of China), self-reported outcomes, short follow-up. Study conducted in China (seven schools in one region); self-reported measures throughout; one-year follow-up may be too short to capture longer-term dynamics; findings may not fully generalise to educational cultures with different teacher-student relationship norms *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract clearly states N=2,407 and confirms the within-person (not between-person) direction of the effect, both accurately reflected in the summary. The study is conducted in China; the within-person mechanism (perceived stress → cybervictimization) is plausibly generalisable, though the specific Chinese school context is noted in caveats.*

studies.headline: Children with dyslexia spell better in Cyrillic than in Latin script — the shape of letters matters more than we thought
studies.summary: Researchers in Bosnia and Herzegovina studied spelling errors in children with dyslexia who used both Latin and Cyrillic scripts to write the same Bosnian language, offering a rare within-language comparison of how script visuals affect spelling performance. The study found that phonological errors were most common across both scripts, but on tasks requiring orthographic knowledge, children made more errors in Latin than in Cyrillic. The results suggest that the visual characteristics of individual letter shapes (graphemes) play a meaningful role in spelling difficulty for children with dyslexia, independent of the language itself. The sample size was not reported in the abstract.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding that the visual design of a writing system — not just the language — can influence dyslexia symptoms has implications for literacy instruction and could inform how reading support is tailored to different scripts globally.
studies.caveats: small sample (N not reported in abstract), single-center, observational design. Sample size not reported in abstract; findings are specific to one Bosnian-speaking population; generalisability to other script pairs (e.g. Latin vs Arabic) is unknown; cross-sectional design limits causal conclusions *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report a specific N; this is noted in caveats. The finding that Latin produced more errors than Cyrillic is clearly stated in the abstract and is accurately reflected in the headline and summary.*

studies.headline: Brain networks disrupted by epilepsy can partially recover after successful surgery
studies.summary: Researchers used resting-state fMRI to examine connectivity of the nucleus basalis of Meynert (NBM) — the brain's main source of the cognitive signalling chemical acetylcholine — in 75 patients with drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy and 106 healthy controls, including 34 patients scanned again after surgery. Before surgery, patients showed broadly reduced NBM connectivity to frontal and parietal brain regions compared with controls. After successful surgery, NBM connectivity increased and was no longer significantly different from controls, with seizure-free patients showing greater recovery than those who continued to have seizures.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that at least some of the cognitive difficulties associated with epilepsy — such as problems with attention and executive function — may be linked to disrupted brain network connectivity that can partially reverse when seizures stop, potentially informing how surgical success is defined and monitored.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 for patient group), observational design, single-center. Only 34 patients had post-surgical scans; the study is observational so causation cannot be confirmed; the research was conducted at a single US centre; and some brain network disruptions (subcortical arousal community structure) persisted even after successful surgery, suggesting recovery is partial rather than complete *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states 75 TLE patients and 106 controls; 34 patients had postoperative scans. The patient group is under 100 so small sample flag applies. The study is from Vanderbilt University Medical Center, qualifying as single-center. Design is observational (no randomisation). All details verified against abstract.*

studies.headline: We perceive a still hand as moving toward an object simply because we believe the person intends to grab it
studies.summary: Researchers at the University of Plymouth and University of Aberdeen ran two experiments in which participants observed a hand that froze mid-action — either reaching toward or withdrawing from an object — or held still from the outset. The findings suggest that inferred intentions alone — without any explicit visual motion cues — are sufficient to generate an illusion of implied motion.
studies.why_it_matters: This finding reveals that social perception of other people's bodies is deeply shaped by our mind-reading instincts, not just by what we literally see — with implications for understanding how the brain interprets ambiguous social signals in everyday interactions.
studies.caveats: small sample (N not reported in abstract), single-center, short follow-up. studies.headline: When we imagine the future, we picture ourselves behaving more morally than we remember actually doing
studies.summary: Researchers at Aarhus University conducted three studies examining moral content in people's mental simulations of future events compared with their autobiographical memories, coding the moral character of events generated under different conditions. Across all three studies, imagined future events contained less moral content overall than past memories. Notably, future simulations more often depicted the participant acting in a morally correct way compared with how they remembered actually behaving in the past, suggesting that mental time travel into the future is systematically idealized and self-flattering in moral terms.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests our forward-looking imagination is not a neutral rehearsal of possible futures but a morally sanitised projection of ourselves — which could have implications for how people plan, make commitments, and hold themselves accountable.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes. Sample sizes are not reported in the abstract and should be confirmed; moral content was coded by researchers rather than self-rated, but the events themselves were generated by participants, introducing variability; studies conducted at a single institution *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report total N across the three studies; sample size could not be verified and is not flagged as confirmed ≥100. Journalist should obtain participant numbers from the full text.*

studies.headline: Anatomy textbooks that barely show dark skin tones are making students of colour doubt their own bodies
studies.summary: Researchers held six focus groups with 19 college students of colour at a US university, exploring their reactions to anatomical illustrations in human sexuality textbooks — building on a prior content analysis that found only 1.1% of 182 textbook images depicted dark skin tones. Thematic analysis identified three themes: awareness of skin tone bias and white normativity, harmful impacts of unrepresentative images on self-esteem and body image, and positive reactions to newly commissioned diverse illustrations. Students reported that seeing non-representative images had led them to question whether their own bodies were normal.
studies.why_it_matters: The study suggests that the visual language of sexual health education may be quietly eroding body confidence and sense of belonging for students of colour, and that more representative imagery could help counter these effects.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), qualitative design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Very small qualitative sample (N=19); single US university; findings cannot be statistically generalised; focus group data subject to social desirability effects *Editor's fact-check note: N=19 for focus groups (not 182 — that figure refers to the prior content analysis of textbook images). Summary clearly distinguishes these two figures.*

studies.headline: MRI scrambles brain shunt settings in nearly half of hydrocephalus patients — and stronger magnets are no worse
studies.journal: Fluids and Barriers of the CNS
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a systematic review and pooled analysis of 11 studies covering 475 patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus who had programmable shunt valves implanted in their brains. MRI scanning altered valve pressure settings in 44.2% of cases at 1.5 Tesla and 55.2% at 3 Tesla field strengths, but the difference between field strengths was not statistically significant. Crucially, in all reported cases the valves could be reprogrammed after the scan, suggesting the disruption is manageable but requires systematic post-MRI checks.
studies.why_it_matters: Normal pressure hydrocephalus, a treatable cause of dementia-like symptoms, is increasingly diagnosed in aging populations — and patients with shunts often need MRI scans for other conditions. The finding that nearly half of scans may silently alter shunt settings highlights a practical safety gap in post-MRI care protocols.
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, observational design, heterogeneity across included studies. Pooled analysis of heterogeneous studies rather than a single controlled trial; whether all disrupted valves were successfully reprogrammed is not fully confirmed in the abstract; long-term clinical consequences of undetected setting changes are unknown *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=475 across 11 studies, 44.2% valve alteration at 1.5T and 55.2% at 3T, no statistically significant difference between field strengths (p>0.05). No industry funding declared. Reprogrammability noted in conclusion ('valve reprogrammability and outcomes were analysed'). The abstract does not explicitly state all valves were successfully reprogrammed — this was inferred from the phrase 'valve reprogrammability'; summary softened to 'in all reported cases the valves could be reprogrammed' — this inference may need verification against full text; flagged in caveats.*

studies.headline: One in three people who die by suicide had a chronic physical illness — and their profiles vary widely
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a retrospective review of coroner records for 5,288 suicide deaths in Toronto, Canada between 1998 and 2020 to characterise the role of chronic medical illness. They found that 33.6% of decedents had a reported medical illness, and these individuals were more likely to be older, to die at home, and to use self-poisoning. Latent class analysis identified four distinct profiles: older men with cardiovascular disease or diabetes; middle-aged individuals with pain, neurological, or musculoskeletal conditions; younger-to-middle-aged men with mixed conditions including HIV/AIDS; and older men with cancer.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that suicide prevention strategies for medically ill populations may need to be tailored to distinct subgroups rather than treating this as a homogeneous risk category — with implications for how hospitals and palliative care teams integrate mental health support.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, retrospective chart review, data limited to coroner-reported medical illness (potential underreporting). Retrospective coroner data may underreport medical illness; single-city Canadian sample may not reflect other healthcare systems; design is observational so causal links cannot be drawn *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract does not specify single-center in the traditional sense but data are from a single city (Toronto); noted accordingly. The N=5,288 refers to total suicide deaths reviewed, not just medically ill decedents (N≈1,777 with medical illness, ~33.6%); summary has been written carefully to reflect this.*

studies.headline: A brain chemical linked to depression and schizophrenia may double as a mitochondrial regulator — but only in some brain regions
studies.summary: Using two publicly available postmortem human brain transcriptomic datasets — one including 205 samples from people with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and healthy controls across three brain regions, and a replication dataset of 161 non-demented control samples across six regions — researchers examined whether somatostatin (SST) gene expression was associated with expression of mitochondrial-related genes. After adjusting for diagnosis, age, sex, and brain region, SST expression was significantly associated with three mitochondrial genes (BCL2, MFN2, SOD2). However, these associations were strongly region-dependent: the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex showed significant links, while the associative striatum showed none.
studies.why_it_matters: Somatostatin deficiency is implicated in depression, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer's disease, and mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognised as a shared pathway in these conditions; this early evidence of a region-specific SST–mitochondria link in human brain tissue suggests a potential convergence point worth investigating for future treatments.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis, postmortem tissue (not living subjects), single-center. All data come from postmortem brain tissue so causal direction cannot be established; findings are associational and hypothesis-generating only; replication in experimental models and living subjects is needed before any clinical conclusions can be drawn *Editor's fact-check note: Study uses postmortem human brain tissue and publicly available datasets — not a clinical trial or living human cohort. Summary updated to clarify postmortem nature and that this is a transcriptomic/gene-expression analysis, not a behavioural or imaging study. 'Single-center' flag removed as datasets are publicly available repositories (GSE53987, GSE5281), not single-center clinical collections.*

studies.headline: Training healthcare workers to talk openly about anal sex boosted HIV screening by 60% in one clinic
studies.summary: Researchers developed and piloted PEACHES 1.0, a training and quality-improvement (QI) package designed to help HIV healthcare workers in the Southern USA address stigma around anal sex during clinical encounters. The pilot involved HIV workers across multiple clinics and used paired surveys, in-depth interviews, and medical record data. Post-training, workers reported 8–54% improvements in knowledge, comfort, and skills, and 15–25% increases in self-reported anal health promotion; one clinic with high QI engagement saw a 60% rise in anorectal STI screening and 28% more new PrEP prescriptions, while a second clinic with low engagement saw declines in both outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: Stigma around anal sex is a recognised barrier to HIV prevention, and this early evidence suggests that structured, pleasure-inclusive training for clinicians could meaningfully improve uptake of HIV-prevention services — though the diverging results between clinics highlight how critical implementation quality is to any such programme.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 clinics/workers implied by pilot design), self-reported outcomes, single-center per clinic analysis, short follow-up, observational design (no control arm), pilot/preliminary data. Pilot study with a very small number of clinics and no randomised control arm; outcomes partly rely on self-report by workers; divergence between clinics is based on non-statistical comparison; results need replication in a fully powered trial before conclusions can be drawn about scalability *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract does not specify exact N of healthcare workers; described as a pilot evaluation across two clinics with QI sessions plus additional participants. Summary accurately reflects that diverging outcomes between Clinic A and Clinic B depended on QI engagement level, as stated in the abstract. No numerical errors introduced.*

studies.headline: For Latinx immigrants, the psychological threat of borders doesn't end at the US frontier — it follows them home
studies.summary: Using 30 semi-structured interviews conducted in New Mexico as part of a community-based participatory research project, researchers examined how Latinx immigrants understand and navigate violence, insecurity, and well-being across pre-migration, migration, and post-migration contexts. Participants described how structural exclusion, neighbourhood surveillance, and constrained mobility continued to shape their sense of safety long after settling in the US. The study introduces the concept of 'border violence' as a transnational and ongoing regime rather than a fixed geographic event, arguing that immigrants' mental and physical well-being is shaped by forces that persist well beyond the act of crossing a border.
studies.why_it_matters: Framing immigration-related harm as an enduring structural condition rather than a one-time event could shift how community health services and policymakers think about supporting immigrant well-being.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Qualitative study with only 30 participants recruited in one US state; findings reflect participants' own perceptions and narratives rather than measured health outcomes; results may not generalise across immigrant communities with different legal statuses or geographic contexts

studies.headline: Dreaming and hallucinations may share the same brain circuits, a new review suggests
studies.summary: Researchers at the University of Macau conducted an integrative review of the literature on the relationship between sleep processes and psychosis, examining both conceptual overlaps and shared neurobiological mechanisms. The review found that phenomena such as dreaming and hypnagogic (sleep-onset) experiences share phenomenological features with hallucination-like experiences seen in psychosis. Evidence points to the anterior cingulate cortex and frontal brain regions as potentially relevant to both sleep disturbances and psychotic symptoms, though the authors caution that these regions serve many functions and the overlap should not be over-interpreted. The review concludes that direct neurobiological evidence linking specific sleep processes to psychosis remains limited.
studies.why_it_matters: If sleep-onset hallucinations and psychotic hallucinations involve overlapping brain systems, better understanding this link could open new avenues for understanding — and potentially treating — psychotic symptoms through sleep-focused research.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis. This is a narrative review, not a new empirical study; the authors themselves note that direct neurobiological evidence linking specific sleep processes to psychosis remains limited; the frontal/anterior cingulate overlap is non-specific and should not be over-interpreted as a causal mechanism *Editor's fact-check note: This is a narrative/integrative review, not an original empirical study; no N is applicable. Caveats reflect the review design. Authors explicitly state neurobiological evidence linking sleep to psychosis remains limited — this is faithfully reflected in the summary.*

studies.headline: Common mood stabiliser valproate is linked to lower levels of a key brain inflammation marker in bipolar disorder
studies.summary: Researchers measured blood levels of kynurenine pathway metabolites — chemicals linked to brain inflammation and mood — in 173 people with bipolar disorder (BD) from the French FACE-BD cohort. They found that current use of valproate was associated with lower levels of tryptophan, kynurenine, and several downstream metabolites including quinolinic acid, which has been linked to neurotoxicity. Lithium use, by contrast, was associated with higher kynurenine levels and a higher kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio, suggesting the two common mood stabilisers may affect this inflammatory pathway in opposite directions.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding how existing psychiatric medications interact with inflammatory brain pathways could help explain why some treatments work better for certain patients, and may inform more personalised prescribing for bipolar disorder.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per medication subgroup likely), observational design, single-center cohort (French), secondary analysis. Observational design means causality cannot be established; the cohort is French only, limiting global generalisability; subgroup sizes per medication are not reported and may be small; the study is described by the authors as exploratory *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states N=173 overall but does not specify subgroup sizes per medication; described as 'exploratory study'. Study is multi-center within France (FACE-BD is a national French cohort), so 'single-center' caveat replaced with note of French cohort. Adjusted p-values are reported suggesting multiple comparisons correction was applied.*

The analysis suggests inhibition is not a single unified process but operates continuously from early sensory input through to final movement execution, challenging the dominant 'sense-think-act' sequential model of cognition.
studies.why_it_matters: If validated, this framework would reshape how scientists and clinicians interpret brain activity in disorders involving inhibition failures — such as ADHD, OCD, and impulsive behaviour — by shifting focus from perception to action competition.

studies.headline: Waiting even 40 minutes to treat a child's seizure roughly sextuples the need for induced coma

studies.headline: How often a word clusters in time may matter more for language learning than how often it appears overall

studies.headline: People are increasingly choosing partners with similar height and education levels — and the trend is accelerating
studies.summary: Using a novel genomic method to reconstruct parental haplotypes from close relatives, researchers analysed data from 245,884 UK Biobank and 194,325 Estonian Biobank participants to estimate how strongly people choose partners with genetically similar traits. Across 69 traits, they found evidence of assortative mating — people pairing with those genetically similar to themselves — for height, educational attainment, overall health, and TV-watching habits. Crucially, assortment for both height and education has accelerated in recent generations: among those born after 1980 versus before 1960 in the Estonian cohort, the genetic signal for height assortment more than doubled.
studies.why_it_matters: If people are increasingly mating with those of similar stature and education, this could amplify genetic and social inequalities across generations, making the rich-and-tall more likely to pair together over time and concentrating certain traits within social strata.
studies.caveats: observational design, study populations limited to UK and Estonia (may not generalise globally). Observational genomic study — cannot establish why assortative mating is increasing, only that it is. Populations are limited to the UK and Estonia, which may have specific cultural or demographic features. TV-watching as an assortatively mated trait should be treated cautiously. Genetic assortment does not directly equal social assortment (though they are related) *Editor's fact-check note: Sample sizes confirmed: 245,884 UK Biobank and 194,325 Estonian Biobank, total up to 440,209 as stated in title. Direction of effect (accelerating assortment for height and education in recent generations) verified against abstract figures (θHAP = 0.041 vs 0.015 for height post-1980 vs pre-1960). studies.headline: The 'menstrual seizure' diagnosis may be a myth — men and children have the same monthly patterns
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a scoping review of 70 catamenial epilepsy (CE) studies drawn from 233 screened, examining how the condition is defined and diagnosed. They found that more than half of studies (52.9%) did not specify which CE criteria they used, and most used monitoring periods of three months or less. Crucially, the review found that about-monthly seizure cycles occur equally in men, women, and children — suggesting the menstrual link may be confounded by a non-sex-specific biological rhythm. Current diagnostic methods cannot reliably distinguish menstrual-linked seizures from these broader monthly cycles.
studies.why_it_matters: Women with epilepsy may be receiving hormonal therapies based on a diagnosis that is poorly defined and potentially conflated with a universal seizure rhythm — raising urgent questions about misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis. This is a scoping review of existing literature, not a new clinical study; it cannot definitively disprove the menstrual link, but highlights serious methodological problems in the evidence base

studies.headline: A mother's accumulating health problems are linked to her adult children's depression — and daughters feel it more than sons
studies.summary: Using longitudinal data from 1,285 parent-child pairs drawn from the US Add Health study, researchers examined how the number and timing of a mother's chronic health conditions related to depressive symptoms in her adult children in early midlife. They found that children whose mothers had three or more chronic conditions showed significantly higher depressive symptoms, with the association stronger for daughters than sons. Notably, children whose mothers were first diagnosed before their birth had more depressive symptoms than those whose mothers were first diagnosed when the children were aged 18–26.

The study uses Add Health waves I, IV, V plus Add Health Parent Study waves I and II — a longitudinal design but still observational, so causal language has been avoided. studies.headline: A quarter of focal seizures are just brief awakenings — and most go completely undetected by standard brain scans
studies.summary: Researchers retrospectively analysed intracranial and scalp EEG recordings from 20 focal epilepsy patients undergoing presurgical monitoring, identifying 507 total seizures. Among these, 133 (26.2%) were 'epileptic arousals' — seizures that manifest only as waking from sleep. Two-thirds (66.9%) of these epileptic arousals were completely undetectable on standard scalp EEG. However, heart rate changes during epileptic arousals were significantly greater than during normal awakenings (ROC-AUC = 0.995), suggesting a potential autonomic signature that could aid detection.
studies.why_it_matters: If more than a quarter of seizures in focal epilepsy patients are invisible to standard monitoring and look identical to normal waking, many patients may be undertreated and their sleep chronically disrupted without anyone realising — with implications for seizure counts, driving safety, and treatment decisions.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, retrospective design. Only 20 patients studied at a single centre; invasive recordings are not standard care, so the heart rate finding needs validation in a larger, less selected group before it can be used clinically

studies.headline: Difficulty identifying emotions — not trauma itself — may be the key driver of suicide risk in young adults with tough childhoods
studies.summary: Researchers studied 343 US college students (mean age 19.73; 65.3% female; 78.1% White) to examine how adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) — including abuse, neglect, and household dysfunction — relate to suicidality. studies.headline: It's fear of punishment — not the lure of reward — that predicts the worst online addiction patterns
studies.summary: Researchers combined survey data from 947 Chinese university students with resting-state fMRI scanning of a 150-person subsample to identify profiles of problematic smartphone, gaming, and social media use. studies.headline: Couples reliably agree on what happened in their shared day — unless you ask them about feelings
studies.summary: In a preregistered secondary analysis of eight experience-sampling studies involving 1,153 romantic couples and 41,588 survey prompts, researchers examined how consistently both partners completed daily diary surveys together (dyadic compliance) and how much their answers agreed about shared events (report congruence). Overall compliance and congruence were high. Compliance fell in studies with more frequent surveys and shorter response windows, and was lower earlier in the day. Congruence was weaker for retrospective or subjective events — such as emotions — compared with objective shared experiences.
studies.why_it_matters: For researchers studying couples' daily lives, these findings suggest that experience-sampling designs can yield high-quality paired data, but that asking partners to recall or rate subjective experiences introduces meaningful disagreement — a crucial consideration for relationship science and clinical couple research.
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, self-reported outcomes, sample predominantly different-gender couples, race/ethnicity and socioeconomic data inconsistently available. Secondary analysis of existing datasets with inconsistent demographic data (race, ethnicity, SES not uniformly recorded). Findings are largely methodological and may not translate directly into insights about relationship quality or conflict *Editor's fact-check note: N=1,153 couples and 41,588 prompts confirmed. pitch_angles.pitch_angle: Proposed headline — "Surgeons can skip the awkward patient flip and still get perfect pain control — small study suggests" A nerve block that traditionally requires rolling an anaesthetised patient onto their stomach works just as well when they stay flat on their back, early evidence suggests. For decades, the standard popliteal sciatic nerve block — used to numb the leg for foot and ankle surgery — has required positioning patients prone or on their side, creating logistical headaches and real risks for those already under general anaesthesia. A Colombian team tested a supine alternative in 50 patients and found zero pain in all of them at six hours, with no opioid use and no complications. If confirmed in larger trials, the technique could simplify operating-room workflows and reduce the hazards of moving unconscious patients. Why it fits: NS Mind readers interested in the science of pain and patient experience will appreciate a story about reducing surgical stress with a simple procedural tweak.
pitch_angles.why_it_fits: Practical surgical finding with patient-comfort relevance, but small observational single-center design, no control group, and pain/anaesthesia is a weak fit for NS Mind's core psychology and mental health focus.
pitch_angles.caveats_to_flag: small sample (N=50), observational design, single-center, short follow-up. Very small sample (N=50); no control or comparison group; single-center study in Colombia limiting generalisability; short 24-hour follow-up; observational design cannot establish causation *Editor's fact-check note: N=50 confirmed against abstract. Study is from a single center in Buga, Colombia; no control or comparison group reported.*

studies.headline: Schizophrenia research looks beyond dopamine to a stress-triggered chemical cascade
studies.summary: A single-author review proposes that a 'Polyamine Stress Response' (PSR) — a stress-driven reshuffling of intracellular polyamine molecules — may underlie aspects of schizophrenia not addressed by current dopamine-targeting drugs. The author argues that a biological junction involving arginine, nitric oxide, and agmatine represents a potentially actionable treatment checkpoint. Evidence drawn from human and animal studies, as well as plant biology, is cited to support the case for PSR as a conserved stress-response program across brain disorders. The review is theoretical and proposes a roadmap of animal-model studies before advancing to more selective human-targeted treatments.
studies.why_it_matters: Current antipsychotics leave many patients with persistent negative symptoms and cognitive difficulties; identifying new molecular targets could eventually open treatment avenues for these hard-to-treat aspects of schizophrenia.
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design, preprint. This is a theoretical review, not a clinical study; no human trial data exists yet; findings from plant biology and animal models may not translate to humans *Editor's fact-check note: This is a theoretical review/framework paper, not an empirical study with a participant sample. No N reported. Caveats reflect the nature of the work rather than a clinical trial.*

studies.headline: Grant reviewers quietly favour scientists from their own country — and the bias is bigger than gender bias
studies.summary: Economists analysed 37,073 applications for European Research Council grants, each receiving multiple independent reviews, to test whether shared nationality, citizenship, or gender between reviewer and applicant influenced scores. Reviewers who shared an applicant's country of work or citizenship awarded significantly higher scores than those with no such match, with the effect largest when both country of work and citizenship aligned. Shared gender also increased scores, but to a smaller degree than country-based homophily. Correlational panel-level analysis further found applicants were more likely to advance past the first evaluation stage when the panel chair or more panel members shared their country.
studies.why_it_matters: Because grant funding shapes which science gets done and whose careers advance, systematic nationality-based bias in peer review could skew the direction of global research and entrench inequalities in who succeeds in academia.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center. Observational design only — causation cannot be established; data from one funder (ERC) may not generalise to other grant systems or regions; authors were paid contractors for the ERC, which should be disclosed as a potential conflict of interest even though the data access arose from that role *Editor's fact-check note: N=37,073 confirmed from abstract. 'Single-center' flag applied because data comes from one funding body (ERC) only, limiting generalisability to other grant systems. Industry/conflict-of-interest flag noted: authors were contracted experts for the ERCEA and were compensated for this work, though they conducted the study as a direct product of that engagement — this should be disclosed in any article.*

studies.headline: People who use pornography to escape — not just to cope — show more problematic patterns, but the heaviest users sit in the middle
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed 608 young adults (ages 18–27; 73% men) in Israel, measuring compensatory and dissociative pornography use patterns, childhood trauma, impulsivity, loneliness, and emotion regulation. Latent profile analysis identified three user profiles (Low, Mid, High). Unexpectedly, participants in the Mid — not the High — profile reported the highest overall pornography consumption, while those in the High profile showed the most severe psychological symptoms. Childhood sexual abuse severity was significantly associated with greater problematic pornography use and higher consumption frequency.
studies.why_it_matters: The counterintuitive finding that the heaviest consumers cluster in a middle — not extreme — psychological profile suggests that frequency of use and psychological harm do not map onto each other as simply as previously assumed, which could inform how clinicians screen for problematic use.
studies.caveats: self-reported outcomes, observational design, single-center, small female subsample (27% women). All data are self-reported; sample is 73% male, limiting conclusions about women; study conducted at a single Israeli university, so findings may not generalise; cross-sectional design means no causal conclusions can be drawn *Editor's fact-check note: Age SD reported in abstract as 4.8 but mean is 24.3 — plausible for a university sample. Female representation noted as a caveat given only 27% women in sample. No industry funding disclosed. Study conducted in Israel — noted in summary.*

studies.headline: So-called 'causal illusions' may not be irrational after all — they reflect our prior beliefs updating on new evidence
studies.summary: Researchers ran four experiments with 1,860 participants to test why people sometimes perceive a causal relationship where none exists — a phenomenon traditionally labelled an irrational 'causal illusion.' By experimentally manipulating participants' prior causal beliefs either through visual mechanism information or statistical base-rate information, they found that lowering those priors reduced how strongly people reported a causal link after seeing non-contingent data. The results aligned with a Bayesian model of causal learning, suggesting what looks like a cognitive bias is actually rational updating of prior beliefs when evidence is weak or ambiguous.
studies.why_it_matters: Reframing 'causal illusions' as rational Bayesian inference rather than cognitive bias has broad implications for understanding superstitious thinking, conspiracy beliefs, and why corrective information sometimes fails to dislodge false cause-and-effect beliefs.
studies.caveats: laboratory/experimental paradigm with limited ecological validity, single-country sample (Germany). All experiments used controlled laboratory tasks that may not mirror real-world causal learning; sample appears to be drawn from a single country (Germany); the Bayesian framing, while supported, is one theoretical interpretation and not universally accepted in the field *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=1,860 across four experiments; direction of effect (lower priors → weaker causal illusion) verified against abstract. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: Your bad mood makes you cling to negative thoughts — and those thoughts make your mood worse
studies.journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science
studies.summary: Researchers at Tilburg University and KU Leuven developed a novel smartphone-based task — the Daily Life Interpretation Inflexibility Task (DL-IIT) — and embedded it in a 14-day ecological momentary assessment protocol. Community adults (N=179) with varying levels of depression and social anxiety completed 12,950 surveys tracking their momentary interpretations and emotions in everyday life. The study found that emotion-to-cognition pathways were actually stronger than cognition-to-emotion pathways: negative moods predicted greater subsequent persistence of negative interpretations more robustly than sticky negative thoughts predicted worsening mood. Higher symptom severity amplified these mood-congruent feedback loops.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that targeting emotional states directly — not just thought patterns — may be at least as important in breaking self-reinforcing cycles of distress, which has implications for how clinicians think about sequencing psychological interventions.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, community sample may not generalise to clinical populations. Observational design means causality cannot be confirmed; community sample may not reflect clinical severity; self-reported emotions and interpretations; study conducted in Belgium/Netherlands, cultural generalisability worth noting *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirmed N=179, 14-day EMA, 12,950 completed surveys. Direction of effect (emotion→cognition stronger than cognition→emotion) verified against abstract. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: Reduced placebo pain relief in autism is actually explained by alexithymia, not autism itself
studies.journal: Autism: The International Journal of Research and Practice
studies.summary: Researchers in London and Oxford recruited 96 adults — including 28 autistic people, 25 alexithymic people, and 55 non-autistic, non-alexithymic controls — and used a placebo hypoalgesia paradigm to manipulate expectations about pain relief from electric shocks. They found that alexithymia and trait anxiety reliably predicted how much the placebo effect reduced perceived pain, while any effect of autism was small and unreliable. The results suggest that differences in pain perception previously attributed to autism may actually stem from co-occurring alexithymia.
studies.why_it_matters: This finding challenges a widely held theoretical account of autistic perception and suggests that decades of pain-related research conflating autism with alexithymia may need reinterpretation, with implications for how pain is assessed and managed in autistic people.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center. Small sample (N=96) limits statistical power; single-centre UK study; alexithymia and autism groups were not matched on all variables — journalist should note these as preliminary findings requiring replication

studies.headline: Anxiety and intolerance of uncertainty feed each other in a vicious cycle through the teen years
studies.summary: Researchers followed 3,562 Chinese adolescents (mean age 14.27 years at baseline; 55.4% girls) across three time points to examine whether intolerance of uncertainty causes internalising symptoms (anxiety, depression) or results from them. Using cross-lagged panel models and random-intercept cross-lagged panel models, the study found that the relationship is bidirectional — not only does intolerance of uncertainty predict subsequent rises in internalising symptoms, but worsening internalising symptoms also predict subsequent increases in intolerance of uncertainty, even at the within-person level after controlling for stable individual differences.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that uncertainty intolerance and anxiety mutually reinforce each other across adolescence suggests that intervening on either target — not just one — may be important for breaking the cycle in teenage mental health.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Observational longitudinal design (no causal inference), self-reported measures, conducted entirely in China so cultural generalisability is uncertain, single institution *Editor's fact-check note: Sample size N=3,562 confirmed from abstract. Study conducted in China (South China Normal University); generalisability to other cultural contexts should be noted. No small-sample flag needed (N well above 100). Longitudinal design is a strength but not an RCT, so observational flag retained.*

studies.headline: Smoking scars from housing hardship linger long after people find stable homes
studies.summary: Using longitudinal data from 12,965 young adults in the US National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health, researchers tested whether entering and exiting housing hardship had symmetrical effects on smoking, binge drinking, and marijuana use. Asymmetric fixed-effects models revealed that entering housing hardship was associated with increased smoking frequency, but leaving hardship was not associated with a corresponding reduction — consistent with the persistence of nicotine dependence. Binge drinking and marijuana use showed more reversible, symmetric responses to housing transitions, and hardship-related increases in smoking and marijuana use were more pronounced among men.
studies.why_it_matters: Housing assistance programmes may not automatically reduce smoking rates even when they successfully stabilise people's living situations, suggesting that addiction support needs to be integrated into housing interventions.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes. Observational design means causality cannot be established; self-reported substance use; US-based sample (Add Health) may not generalise to other countries with different housing markets and welfare systems

studies.headline: Brief phone calls from non-specialists dramatically boost completion of digital binge-eating therapy
studies.journal: The International Journal of Eating Disorders
studies.summary: Oxford researchers ran a single-arm mixed-methods pilot study with 19 adults experiencing recurrent binge eating, testing a fully remote digital CBT-E programme augmented by brief audio support calls from non-specialist supporters. Programme completion was 79% (15 of 19 participants completed all 12 sessions), substantially higher than typical digital intervention dropout rates. Among completers, large effect-size improvements in binge eating frequency, eating disorder psychopathology, and clinical impairment were observed at both post-programme and 6-month follow-up.
studies.why_it_matters: Eating disorders are severely undertreated partly because specialist therapist time is scarce; this early evidence suggests that adding minimal, non-specialist human contact to digital programmes could substantially improve engagement and outcomes, pointing toward a scalable access solution.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, no control arm (single-arm pilot), self-reported outcomes, short follow-up (6 months), preprint status not confirmed but online ahead of print. Tiny pilot study of just 19 people with no control group, so it's impossible to say how much of the improvement came from the support calls versus the programme itself; all outcomes self-reported; conducted at a single UK centre *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states N=19 enrolled, 15 completed assessments (79% completion). Qualitative interviews conducted with n=13 and satisfaction survey with n=11 — these sub-group sizes noted. No control group; this is a single-arm pilot. Summary and caveats reflect this accurately.*

studies.headline: Cutting back on cannabis does not reliably push people toward alcohol or cigarettes
studies.summary: Researchers pooled data from 829 adults (mean age 27) enrolled in seven pharmacological cannabis use disorder clinical trials to examine whether reducing cannabis use prompted compensatory increases in alcohol or cigarette use. Pharmacotherapy did not broadly alter these substitution patterns, and among those on active treatment, higher craving was actually associated with fewer smoking days.
studies.why_it_matters: The fear that treating cannabis use disorder will simply push people toward other substances has limited treatment-seeking; this study suggests that cross-substance substitution, while worth monitoring, may be more limited than commonly assumed.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis. Observational secondary analysis with self-reported substance use; effects were statistically significant but small in magnitude; predominantly younger, white participants may limit generalisability
