studies.headline: Brain stimulation boosts spatial memory — but only the first time you try it
studies.summary: Researchers applied 6 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) to the fronto-parietal network of participants in a within-subjects design across four sessions, measuring visuospatial working memory using the Corsi Block Tapping Task. No effects on response speed were found.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that brain stimulation's memory benefits rapidly diminish with repeated sessions suggests current tACS protocols may need redesigning before they can be used reliably in therapeutic or cognitive-enhancement contexts.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up. studies.headline: Most patients become briefly confused after electroconvulsive therapy — but nearly all recover within 30 minutes

studies.headline: Stigma and mistrust — not lack of awareness — are the main barriers stopping gay and bisexual men from taking HIV prevention pills

Using a Social-Ecological Model and Intersectionality Framework, they found that barriers included low perceived HIV risk, stigma, healthcare mistrust, limited provider engagement, and financial constraints. Intersecting social identities — including ethnicity, religion, relationship status, and socioeconomic status — shaped how these barriers operated, suggesting a one-size-fits-all approach to PrEP promotion is unlikely to reach the most marginalised groups.
studies.why_it_matters: Despite PrEP being highly effective at preventing HIV, uptake remains inequitable; this review suggests structural and identity-based factors — not just individual knowledge gaps — are driving the disparity, with implications for how public health campaigns are designed.
studies.caveats: small sample (13 studies reviewed), observational design, scoping review (not systematic meta-analysis), heterogeneous study populations. Only 13 studies were included and this is a scoping — not systematic — review, so no statistical pooling of effects was possible; findings are synthesised qualitatively and may not reflect the full global evidence base *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms 13 eligible studies included in the review. studies.headline: Babies don't learn to walk in a straight line — their locomotor paths are messy, individual, and surprisingly backwards at times

studies.headline: Racial bias warps face-reading — Black faces trigger fear-based distrust, not anger-based distrust like White faces
studies.summary: Across two pre-registered studies, researchers asked US participants to evaluate the trustworthiness of synthetic Black, White, and East Asian male faces, then used computational models to identify which emotional resemblances drove those judgments (Study 1 Phase I: N=405; Study 2 Phase I: N=436; Phase II ratings: N=194 and N=513). For White faces, perceived untrustworthiness was linked to anger-like features — the well-established pattern. The findings suggest that race fundamentally alters the emotional cues people use to judge whether a face looks trustworthy.
studies.why_it_matters: These findings suggest that the face-reading shortcuts humans use to assess trustworthiness are not universal but racially distorted, with potential implications for understanding racial bias in high-stakes real-world judgments such as hiring, policing, and legal decisions.

Participants were predominantly White Americans (64–72%), so it is unclear whether the same distortions appear in more diverse or non-US samples. Observational design means causation cannot be established *Editor's fact-check note: Sample sizes verified against abstract for all four phase samples. studies.headline: AI reading teens' private texts can predict a depressive episode a week before it happens
studies.journal: Journal of Psychopathology and Clinical Science
studies.summary: Researchers at Columbia University fitted 223 adolescents (mean age 16.4; 37 with current MDD, 103 with remitted MDD, 83 healthy controls) with a smartphone app that captured all keyboard inputs over 12 months — averaging nearly 18,000 text entries per participant — and daily mood ratings. Fine-tuned transformer-based AI models (including GPT-4-mini) were substantially better than traditional rule-based tools at detecting negative self-referential language in the teens' texts. Adolescents with current or remitted depression showed significantly more negative self-referential language than healthy peers, and elevated levels predicted worse mood the next day and a higher likelihood of a depressive episode the following week — though the episode-prediction finding was not robust to all sensitivity analyses.
studies.why_it_matters: If validated at scale, passive analysis of everyday smartphone text could offer an unobtrusive, continuous signal for identifying when a young person's depression risk is rising — potentially enabling earlier intervention without requiring the teenager to self-report symptoms.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per diagnostic group), observational design, self-reported outcomes (mood ratings), single-center, short follow-up relative to depressive course, sensitivity analyses weakened the depressive-episode prediction finding. Observational design cannot prove causation; the week-ahead depressive-episode prediction did not survive all sensitivity analyses; each diagnostic subgroup had fewer than 100 participants; all data came from one research team (Columbia); ethical questions around passive text monitoring of minors are not addressed in the study *Editor's fact-check note: Total N=223 is confirmed in abstract. The abstract explicitly states the association with depressive episodes 'was not robust to sensitivity analyses' — this caveat is included in the summary and caveats as required. The study is described as observational/naturalistic, not an intervention trial.*

studies.headline: Wristwatch data reveals that ADHD hyperactivity ratings only align with real movement later in the school day
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.summary: Using data from 6,518 seven-year-olds in the UK Millennium Cohort Study, researchers compared objective physical activity measured by actigraphy every 15 minutes across the school day with parent and teacher hyperactivity ratings on the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. While both parent and teacher ratings were positively associated with objective movement overall, teacher ratings showed significantly stronger alignment with actual activity in mid-morning and afternoon lessons than in the first lesson of the day. The findings suggest that subjective assessments of hyperactivity may be most accurate after children have had time to settle into the school routine.
studies.why_it_matters: If teacher ratings of hyperactivity are less aligned with objective movement early in the day, this could have implications for how and when ADHD-related observations are collected in school settings, potentially affecting which children are flagged for assessment.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes (informant ratings). Observational design means no causal conclusions can be drawn; informant ratings are inherently subjective; effect sizes, while statistically significant, are small; study is UK-based (Millennium Cohort)

studies.headline: Boys behave worse at school but it barely explains why girls get better grades — something else is driving the gap
studies.summary: Researchers analysed data from 18,234 students (mean age 14.4; 50% female) across 886 classes in England, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden, drawn from the Children of Immigrants Longitudinal Survey in Four European Countries (CILS4EU). The study tested whether boys' higher rates of school resistance behaviour — defying rules, rejecting authority, low effort — could explain why girls tend to get better language grades. Despite resistance behaviour strongly predicting grades, including it in statistical models did not meaningfully close the gender grade gap. A further counterintuitive finding emerged: girls were more harshly penalised academically for resistance behaviour in some countries, which may offset the advantage girls would otherwise gain from boys' worse behaviour. Boys retained an advantage in mathematics grades.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding challenges a widespread assumption in education research — that boys' disruptive behaviour is the key driver of the gender grade gap — and suggests that subtler, possibly teacher-perception-related mechanisms are at work that future research needs to identify.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis. Secondary analysis of existing survey data; resistance behaviour is self-reported by students, which may underestimate actual levels; observational design means causation cannot be inferred; findings are from four European countries and may not generalise elsewhere *Editor's fact-check note: Sample size (N=18,234) and mean age (14.4) confirmed against abstract. The abstract specifies boys hold an advantage in mathematics — this is included in the summary. Secondary analysis of existing CILS4EU data confirmed. Self-reported resistance behaviour noted in abstract. No industry funding declared.*

studies.headline: A general anxiety-and-depression therapy cuts suicidal thoughts more in Hispanic teens than in white peers
studies.summary: Researchers reanalyzed data from a randomized controlled trial of Brief Behavioral Therapy (BBT) — a transdiagnostic treatment targeting both anxiety and depression — to examine whether ethnicity and depression status moderated its effect on suicidal thoughts and behaviors. This is a secondary, hypothesis-generating analysis of archival trial data.
studies.why_it_matters: Hispanic/Latine youth face elevated suicide risk compared with Non-Hispanic White peers, and evidence that a widely available non-suicide-specific therapy may disproportionately reduce that risk in this group could inform how clinicians prioritize and tailor treatment for underserved populations.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per subgroup), secondary analysis, short follow-up, self-reported outcomes. This is a secondary, hypothesis-generating reanalysis of archival trial data, not a pre-registered primary outcome. Confirmatory trials are needed before any clinical recommendations can be made *Editor's fact-check note: The total analytic subsample was n=163, but the key subgroup (depressed Hispanic/Latine youth) is a subset of this, likely well below N=100. studies.headline: Blood-pressure drugs hoped to help psychosis show no mental health benefit in large real-world study
studies.summary: Researchers used English electronic health records (Clinical Practice Research Datalink) to emulate a clinical trial comparing two types of dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers — common blood-pressure medications — in 4,302 people with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or other psychoses. The study tested whether brain-penetrating DHPs reduced psychiatric hospitalisations and self-harm compared to amlodipine (a non-brain-penetrating DHP) over 12 months. The primary analysis found no clear evidence of benefit, and one sensitivity analysis suggested a possible elevated self-harm risk in the brain-penetrating group, though confidence intervals were wide and results were imprecise.
studies.why_it_matters: Calcium channel blockers have attracted interest as potential adjunct treatments for severe mental illness; these findings suggest the brain-penetrating hypothesis does not translate to clear real-world benefit, tempering enthusiasm for repurposing this drug class.
studies.caveats: observational design, imprecise estimates (wide confidence intervals), active comparator design cannot distinguish absence of effect from equivalent benefit of both drugs. Observational design means causation cannot be established; the active-comparator design means the study cannot distinguish between no effect and equivalent benefit in both drug groups; confidence intervals are wide. Results were from English NHS records and may not generalise globally *Editor's fact-check note: Sample size verified: N=918 penetrant DHP group + N=3,384 amlodipine group = 4,302 total. studies.headline: Imperfect AI guidance makes pilots worse at spotting hazards than having no AI at all
studies.summary: Researchers simulated augmented-reality (AR) cueing displays for wide-field visual search tasks — akin to a pilot scanning a runway — in two laboratory experiments. They tested how different cue types (local vs. global, single vs. dual, spatial vs. identity) affected search accuracy and speed under perfect or imperfect automation. When the automation made errors, participants performed worse than if they had received no AI guidance at all, a pattern known as automation bias. Miss-prone automation produced larger response-time costs than false-alarm-prone automation, and dual cues slightly amplified the bias under miss-prone conditions.
studies.why_it_matters: As AR-based AI guidance systems are deployed in high-stakes settings like aviation and security screening, these findings suggest that imperfect automation could actively endanger performance rather than simply failing to help — a key design consideration for engineers and regulators.
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design (laboratory simulation, not real-world task). studies.headline: Adding fun and competition to work at the same time cancels out the benefits of each
studies.summary: Researchers in Romania randomly assigned 195 adults to one of four vignette conditions in a 2×2 factorial experiment, varying whether a described work scenario included fun elements, competitive elements, both, or neither. Participants in 'playful work design' conditions — involving fun, competition, or both — anticipated higher work engagement, task performance, positive affect, and flow compared to controls. studies.headline: The brain's emotion hub works in a hierarchy, not in isolation

The study is entirely computational/meta-analytic and did not recruit participants directly; it re-analysed existing neuroimaging activation data.

studies.headline: Counting red flags — not just spotting one — may be the smarter way to catch serious causes of headache in children
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a single-centre retrospective study of 187 children and adolescents (aged 2–18 years; median age 14.7; 60% female) who attended a Turkish tertiary emergency department and received brain imaging for headache. studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 abnormal cases), observational design, single-center, retrospective, selection bias (imaging-based cohort only), short follow-up. studies.headline: Most Korean teens stay resistant to smoking, but a small group's urge to smoke quietly grows over five years
studies.summary: Researchers tracked smoking susceptibility annually for five years (2019–2023) in a nationally representative sample of 5,045 Korean adolescents, starting from around age 11–12. studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that parental attitudes toward smoking, harm perceptions, and media exposure are modifiable targets for prevention, and that tracking susceptibility over time — rather than at a single snapshot — may better identify at-risk youth before tobacco use begins.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, narrow to Korean adolescent population. studies.headline: Anxiety before surgery raises the odds of needing high-dose oxycodone — but only if you're under 75

studies.headline: Being overly rigid and being impulsive are not two sides of the same coin, study finds

studies.headline: A new model reveals why your eyes jump around the page — and it's surprisingly rational
studies.summary: Researchers developed a computational model of reading based on 'hierarchical resource rationality,' proposing that eye movements during reading are not random or purely reflexive but are optimised to maximise comprehension while minimising cognitive effort and time, operating across three nested levels: individual word fixation, sentence-level integration, and whole-text comprehension. The model — tested against a wide range of empirical findings from human reading studies — successfully replicated patterns from low-level lexical effects to higher-order comprehension outcomes. No single new human participant sample was recruited; instead, the computational model was validated against existing human data from the reading literature.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding reading as a rational, resource-constrained process could inform how we design text, educational tools, and interfaces for people with reading difficulties or cognitive constraints.
studies.caveats: secondary analysis. This is a computational modelling study validated against existing data rather than a new randomised experiment with human participants. studies.headline: Parents unconsciously time their hand gestures to help children predict words they already know
studies.summary: Researchers at University College London annotated 929 representational gestures from 38 caregivers during semi-naturalistic conversations with their 3–4-year-old children (N=38 caregivers). They found that gesture timing was not fixed: for familiar words, caregivers produced the meaningful stroke of a gesture before the word arrived, potentially helping children predict it; for unfamiliar words, the stroke came at the same time as or after the word, providing enriching semantic context instead. Caregivers appeared to make these fine-grained adjustments spontaneously, without conscious instruction.
studies.why_it_matters: This finding suggests that caregivers instinctively calibrate non-verbal cues to a child's vocabulary knowledge, offering a potential new lens on how children learn language and why face-to-face interaction may be hard to replicate digitally.

Observational design means causality (whether the timing actually helps learning) cannot be established *Editor's fact-check note: N=38 caregivers with 929 gestures annotated — the unit of analysis is gestures within a small caregiver sample, so 'small sample' caveat applies to caregivers. studies.headline: Whether numbers feel 'left' or 'right' in your mind depends on what task you're doing, not a fixed mental map
studies.summary: Researchers used behavioural experiments and EEG (event-related potentials) to examine whether the well-known SNARC effect — the tendency to associate small numbers with left space and large numbers with right space — is a fixed mental representation or a flexible one. Participants completed two tasks (parity judgment and magnitude comparison) while brain activity was recorded; sample size is not reported in the abstract. The study found a significant trade-off: the SNARC effect was stronger during explicit magnitude comparison, while a competing spatial effect (SPoARC) dominated during implicit parity judgment. ERP data suggested that explicit numerical tasks recruit additional cognitive resources to activate spatial-number templates from long-term memory.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding challenges the long-held view that our mental number line is a stable, automatic feature of how the brain represents quantity, suggesting instead that it is dynamically constructed depending on cognitive demands — with potential implications for understanding dyscalculia and numerical cognition more broadly.
studies.caveats: small sample (N not reported in abstract), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes not applicable — ERP used. studies.headline: A neglected brainstem region may hold the key to Parkinson's most stubborn symptoms
studies.summary: This comprehensive review examines the pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN), a small brainstem structure involved in locomotion, arousal, and reward, and its role in Parkinson's disease. The authors synthesize neuroanatomical, electrophysiological, and clinical evidence to argue that selective degeneration of specific PPN neuron subtypes drives treatment-resistant gait freezing and falls — symptoms that standard dopamine-based therapies fail to address. The review also critically assesses deep brain stimulation of the PPN as a potential therapy, noting significant challenges in target localization and patient selection.
studies.why_it_matters: Gait freezing and falls are among the most disabling and hardest-to-treat symptoms in advanced Parkinson's disease; understanding the PPN's role could point toward new deep brain stimulation strategies for patients who no longer respond to standard treatment.
studies.caveats: Review paper — no new empirical data collected. studies.headline: Adults can learn perfect pitch faster than thought — but only if you remove a key auditory cue
studies.summary: Researchers in France ran three experiments with non-musicians and musicians to test whether adults could rapidly acquire absolute pitch — the rare ability to name a musical note without a reference tone — using an incidental contingency learning task. The key finding was that learning based on pitch chroma (the note identity, e.g. 'C') was possible but very difficult with normal piano tones because the more salient cue of pitch height (how high or low a note sounds) dominated attention. However, when participants were trained using Shepard tones — synthesised sounds engineered to strip out pitch height — robust learning occurred, suggesting the main barrier to adult absolute pitch acquisition is perceptual competition rather than a hard biological limit. Sample sizes are not reported in the abstract.
studies.why_it_matters: The widespread belief that absolute pitch can only be acquired in early childhood may need revision; the real obstacle could be a learnable perceptual skill rather than a closed developmental window, which has implications for music education and our understanding of auditory plasticity.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, no transfer to real-world instruments found with Shepard tone training. Sample sizes are not reported in the abstract; training with Shepard tones did not transfer to real instruments, so practical musical applications remain unproven; the study was conducted in France with laboratory participants and has not been replicated *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report specific N values for each experiment; 'small sample (N<100)' is flagged as likely given the laboratory task design and typical sample sizes in this literature, but cannot be confirmed precisely from the abstract alone. studies.headline: Brain-wave measurements may reveal what acupuncture actually does to the mind
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a critical narrative review of studies published over the past decade that used endogenous event-related potentials (ERPs) — brain-wave signals measured with millisecond precision — to objectively assess whether acupuncture changes cognitive and emotional processing. The review covered acupuncture trials involving patients with cognitive disorders and neuropsychiatric conditions, examining how different acupoints and stimulation techniques affected ERP components such as P300 and mismatch negativity. Most studies reported improvements in ERP measures following acupuncture, and some found associations between ERP changes and clinical symptom improvement, but the authors caution that serious methodological weaknesses — including high heterogeneity, lack of reliability validation, and confounded combined-treatment designs — mean the findings should be treated as exploratory rather than conclusive.
studies.why_it_matters: As acupuncture is increasingly studied as a complementary approach for conditions like cognitive decline and depression, identifying objective, brain-based markers of its effects could help disentangle genuine neurological changes from placebo responses.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, high methodological heterogeneity across reviewed studies, lack of reliability validation in primary studies. This is a narrative review, not a meta-analysis; primary studies varied widely in design, acupoints used, and patient populations; many lacked sham-acupuncture controls; ERP reliability was rarely validated; and most studies were conducted in China, raising questions about generalisability *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not specify a total participant N across reviewed studies; no N is reported in the review itself, so no sample-size flag was added beyond noting the methodological heterogeneity. studies.headline: It's not how much war coverage you watch that drives trauma symptoms — it's how stressful you find it
studies.journal: Psychological Trauma: Theory, Research, Practice and Policy
studies.summary: Researchers followed 389 Israeli adults with weekly assessments over six weeks during the 2025 Israel-Hamas hostage deal, measuring PTSD symptoms, traditional and social media use for war content, and subjective perceptions of that media exposure. Using multilevel models and time-lagged analyses, the study found that the type of media platform (social vs. traditional) mattered little; instead, whether individuals perceived media exposure as stressful was the strongest predictor of PTSD symptoms. Time-lagged analyses also revealed a bidirectional relationship, with distress and stressful media appraisals mutually reinforcing one another over time, and younger adults showing stronger links between distressing media perceptions and PTSD.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that interventions targeting how people emotionally interpret war-related media — rather than simply reducing screen time — may be more effective for protecting mental health during prolonged crises.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-region population (Israeli adults during a specific conflict), short follow-up. Six-week longitudinal design confirmed. Effect direction confirmed: subjective appraisal, not media type, was the dominant factor. Noted that sample is Israeli adults during a specific conflict — context is relevant but the bidirectional mechanism has plausible universal applicability, so not excluded.*

studies.headline: Family parenting programs quietly improve child outcomes their designers never intended
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, and Allied Disciplines
studies.summary: Researchers systematically screened 2,556 family-centered prevention programs and reviewed 166 against inclusion criteria, ultimately cataloging 24 programs with documented 'crossover effects' — positive outcomes in domains the intervention never specifically targeted. Fourteen of those 24 programs showed significant benefits in at least one unintended area, spanning internalizing problems, externalizing behavior, suicidal thoughts, physical health, academic performance, high-risk sexual behavior, and parental depression. The review suggests these programs may be delivering substantially more value than their headline targets imply.
studies.why_it_matters: If family-based prevention programs routinely improve child and family outcomes beyond their stated goals, policymakers may be systematically undervaluing — and underfunding — some of the most cost-effective mental health interventions available.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis. This is a narrative review of existing programs rather than a new trial; it cannot establish causation. The 24 programs with crossover effects represent a curated subset, and publication bias may mean programs that found no crossover effects are underrepresented *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract describes a registry-based review (not a meta-analysis with pooled statistics), so 'observational design' and 'secondary analysis' are appropriate flags. studies.headline: Personalised micro-interventions tailored to individual emotional networks reduce teacher burnout more than one-size-fits-all approaches
studies.summary: A cluster-randomised trial across 84 public schools in H Province, China, tested whether brief digital micro-interventions chosen to target each teacher's most influential emotional 'nodes' (identified via ecological momentary assessment) outperformed the same interventions delivered in random order. Teachers first completed 14 days of smartphone-based mood tracking, which was used to map individual emotional networks; an algorithm then selected personalised interventions targeting key network points. Over 8 weeks, teachers receiving personalised targeting reported greater happiness (4.4 points higher on a 0–100 scale) and greater reductions in burnout-related network scores than controls, with effects stronger among more conscientious individuals.
studies.why_it_matters: As teacher shortages and burnout worsen globally, this study suggests that personalising digital mental health tools to an individual's emotional profile — rather than delivering generic content — may meaningfully improve wellbeing at scale.
studies.caveats: single-center, conducted in China (H Province only), short follow-up, single-author study, small effect sizes, replication needed. The trial was conducted in a single Chinese province, and results may not generalise to other education systems or cultures. The study has a single author, which raises questions about peer oversight. Effect sizes, while statistically robust, are modest (4.4 points on a 100-point happiness scale). The authors themselves call for replication with longer follow-up before clinical or policy application *Editor's fact-check note: Study is conducted entirely in China (H Province); however, the intervention mechanism (network-informed personalised digital mental health) is universal in principle and the trial design is robust (cluster-RCT, Bayesian multilevel modelling), so it is not excluded on regional grounds. Single-author study flagged as a potential quality concern. Effect size on happiness (4.4 points on 0–100 scale) is statistically credible but modest in practical terms — noted in summary.*

studies.headline: Abuse survivors who internalise their abuser's perspective are at greater risk of lasting depression and anxiety
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed 718 adult female survivors of childhood abuse in Israel, examining two psychological processes: identification with the aggressor (IWA — internalising the abuser's perspective) and doubt about one's own abuse-related perceptions (DARA). Using longitudinal self-report measures at two time points (with n=245 completing follow-up), the study found that higher levels of both IWA and DARA were associated with greater concurrent and subsequent depression and anxiety. Survivors with co-occurring high IWA and DARA showed the highest long-term symptom burden, even after controlling for abuse severity and baseline symptoms.
studies.why_it_matters: These findings suggest that the psychological tendency to identify with one's abuser — and to doubt one's own perceptions of the abuse — may be important targets in therapy for childhood abuse survivors, potentially explaining why some individuals struggle to recover despite treatment.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, short follow-up, female-only sample, conducted in Israel. Study included only adult women in Israel, limiting generalisability across genders and cultures. All measures were self-reported, and a significant proportion of participants did not complete the follow-up survey. Observational design means causality cannot be established *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract specifies female participants only (718 women); summary updated to reflect this. Follow-up sample (n=245) is substantially smaller than baseline — noted in caveats.*

studies.headline: A dopamine gene variant may explain why some people with sleep apnea wake up too easily — and others don't
studies.summary: Researchers in Poland conducted a prospective observational study of 144 adults with polysomnography-confirmed obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), examining whether a variant in the COMT gene (rs4680) — which affects dopamine metabolism — was associated with having a low arousal threshold (waking too easily during breathing disruptions). Of 144 participants, 76 (52.8%) met criteria for a low arousal threshold phenotype. Those with the COMT rs4680 G-allele were more likely to fall into the low-arousal-threshold group, while the AA genotype was more common among those with a high arousal threshold, suggesting dopaminergic pathways may contribute to differences in OSA severity and subtype.
studies.why_it_matters: OSA is increasingly understood as a heterogeneous condition with distinct biological subtypes, and identifying genetic factors linked to arousal threshold could eventually help personalise treatment — for example, by distinguishing patients likely to benefit from therapies targeting arousal rather than airway anatomy.

studies.headline: The standard face-blindness test may be scoring the wrong things, study suggests
studies.summary: Researchers in Japan applied classical test theory and item response theory to evaluate the quality of individual items in the PI20, a widely used 20-item self-report questionnaire for developmental prosopagnosia (face blindness). The study found that items capturing the psychological burden and social consequences of face-processing difficulties were the most precise and informative, while items related to recognising distinctive or familiar faces — including one's own face — contributed least to the overall measure. The results suggest that some PI20 items may not be suitable for screening purposes.
studies.why_it_matters: The PI20 is used by researchers worldwide to identify people with developmental prosopagnosia; if some of its questions are poor discriminators, studies relying on it may be misclassifying participants, affecting everything from prevalence estimates to neuroimaging research.
studies.caveats: self-reported outcomes, single-center, small sample (N not reported in abstract). Sample size not reported in abstract; study is self-report only; conducted in Japan, where cultural norms around face recognition may differ; PI20 was originally developed in English-speaking populations *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report the sample size (N); 'small sample' flag is noted as possible but unverified. studies.headline: A simple hand gesture during seizures could pinpoint a hard-to-find epilepsy hotspot in the brain
studies.summary: Researchers retrospectively analyzed 510 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy treated at Beijing Tiantan Hospital, identifying 34 who displayed the 'Five Sign' — a distinctive ictal hand posture involving full finger extension and spreading. The Five Sign was strongly associated with insulo-opercular (IO) epilepsy, with the highest positive predictive value for IO localization at 64.7%, and its presence significantly increased the likelihood of IO seizure origin. Multimodal brain imaging and stereoelectroencephalography confirmed that the sign reflects engagement of a distributed motor network centered on the posterior insulo-opercular region.
studies.why_it_matters: For patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, identifying the precise brain region generating seizures is critical for surgical planning; a simple observable hand sign that points toward a notoriously difficult-to-localize region could improve presurgical evaluation and potentially surgical outcomes.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, retrospective. Retrospective single-center study from one Chinese hospital; the Five Sign subgroup was only 34 patients; results need prospective validation in diverse populations before clinical adoption *Editor's fact-check note: Total cohort was 510 but only 34 patients exhibited the Five Sign — the relevant sample for the main finding is N=34, flagged as small sample. Single-center study at Beijing Tiantan Hospital noted.*

studies.headline: Listening to the sound of your own breathing helps you recover from stress faster
studies.summary: Researchers at the University of Surrey ran two studies examining whether real-time auditory feedback of nasal breathing (biofeedback) could speed psychological and physiological recovery after mild stress. In the main experiment (N=37), participants completed stress-inducing cognitive tasks and then practised either biofeedback nasal breathing or normal free breathing in a crossover design. studies.why_it_matters: As wearable audio devices become ubiquitous, the finding suggests a simple, scalable stress-recovery technique — hearing your own breath — could be built into everyday technology without requiring training in meditation or formal breathing exercises.

studies.headline: Cutting and repairing a hand nerve reshuffles the brain's finger map — but surprisingly doesn't explain why patients struggle

studies.headline: Clinical trials are measuring patient improvement in at least seven different incompatible ways
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a methodological scoping review of four clinical psychology journals (2020–2023), examining how 226 clinical trials measured whether individual patients improved. Only 29 trials (13%) formally assessed reliable change, and among those, researchers identified at least seven distinct ways of operationalising the same core statistical tool — the Reliable Change Index. These differences in calculation method produced threshold discrepancies as large as 79%, or about one standard deviation, meaning whether a patient is classified as 'reliably improved' can hinge entirely on which version of the formula a researcher chose.
studies.why_it_matters: If clinical trials use incompatible methods to measure individual patient improvement, comparisons across studies — and therefore evidence-based treatment decisions — may be built on shaky statistical ground.
studies.caveats: observational design, secondary analysis. This is a methodological review, not a clinical study — it identifies a problem rather than measuring its real-world harm to patients. Journalists should avoid implying that existing treatment recommendations are wrong, only that comparisons between trials may be less reliable than assumed

studies.headline: A 20-minute play session sharpens preschoolers' ability to sync their senses — and kids with poorest self-control gain the most
studies.summary: Italian researchers tested whether a single 20-minute play-based multisensory training session could improve preschoolers' sensitivity to intersensory synchrony — the ability to detect that sights and sounds belong together in time. The study included 77 trained children aged 3–6 and 62 age-matched controls. Children who received training showed a significantly greater preference for synchronous audiovisual events immediately after, with effects generalising to untrained speech stimuli; notably, children with the lowest inhibitory control showed the largest gains.
studies.why_it_matters: Intersensory synchrony perception is thought to underpin higher-order cognitive development; the finding that a brief, non-verbal play session can strengthen it — especially in children with weaker self-control — suggests a low-cost approach that could benefit children at risk of developmental difficulties.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per group, though combined N=139), single-center, short follow-up. Only immediate post-training effects were measured (no follow-up), the sample was Italian preschoolers from a single centre, and total N was 139 — moderate for a developmental study. Whether gains persist or translate to real-world language and attention outcomes remains unknown *Editor's fact-check note: Combined N is 139 (77 trained + 62 controls), so the per-group N is below 100 but total is above. Noted small sample flag is borderline; retained as a caveat given per-group sizes. No industry funding declared in abstract.*

studies.headline: Brain timing signals run too fast in the cortex and too slow deep down in early schizophrenia — before any medication
studies.summary: Researchers in China used resting-state fMRI to measure intrinsic neural timescales (the natural rhythm of brain activity) in 123 first-episode schizophrenia patients who were drug-naïve or minimally treated, compared with 102 matched healthy controls. They found a striking divergence: cortical brain regions showed shorter-than-normal timescales while subcortical regions showed prolonged timescales, a pattern linked to synapse-related genes and cerebral blood flow. The study suggests this cortical-subcortical mismatch may be a neurobiological signature of schizophrenia that predates medication effects.
studies.why_it_matters: Identifying a reliable brain-based marker of early schizophrenia that is not confounded by medication could accelerate diagnosis and help researchers understand what goes wrong in the brain before illness becomes entrenched.
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design. Single-centre study in China; fMRI measures are indirect proxies for neural activity; Mendelian randomisation was not used so causality cannot be established; clinical translation is distant *Editor's fact-check note: Sample sizes confirmed: 123 patients, 102 controls — total N=225, above the N≥100 threshold. Study conducted at a single centre in Changsha, China. No industry funding declared.*

studies.headline: Longer or earlier smoking medication doesn't help most people quit — but counselling type matters for some
studies.summary: A factorial randomised controlled trial enrolled 496 adult primary care patients (55% women, 45.6% Black) to test four smoking cessation variables: medication type (varenicline vs. combination nicotine replacement therapy), pre-quit medication duration (4 weeks vs. standard 1 week), total medication duration (24 vs. 12 weeks), and counselling intensity (4 vs. 2 sessions). None of the four factors produced statistically significant main effects on biochemically confirmed abstinence at 12, 26, or 52 weeks. However, a three-way interaction suggested that more intensive cessation counselling improved quit rates specifically when varenicline was paired with a longer pre-quit phase — an effect not seen with combination NRT. The trial was stopped early due to pandemic-related budget cuts, falling short of its planned N=608.
studies.why_it_matters: The results challenge the common clinical assumption that longer or earlier pharmacotherapy automatically improves quit rates, suggesting instead that the match between medication type and counselling intensity may matter more than duration alone.
studies.caveats: short of planned sample size (stopped early, N=496 vs planned 608), single-center, short follow-up relative to lifetime smoking risk. The trial was stopped early due to COVID-19 budget cuts and did not reach its planned sample size, meaning it may have been underpowered to detect real effects; the three-way interaction finding should be treated as exploratory; results come from a single US academic centre and may not generalise broadly *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract explicitly states the trial was discontinued before reaching the proposed sample size of 608 due to pandemic-related budgetary constraints; this has been noted in caveats as 'stopped early'. The study was conducted at the University of Wisconsin — described as single-center in design.*

studies.headline: Teaching your brain to ignore certain foods actually makes you want them less, brain scans suggest
studies.summary: Researchers used functional MRI to examine 85 women who underwent food go/no-go training — a task in which participants repeatedly practise responding to some foods and withholding responses to others. After training, participants reported wanting the 'no-go' foods significantly less, and brain imaging showed reduced activity in frontal and visual regions associated with this devaluation effect. Mediation analysis suggested that changes in food wanting were associated with subsequent food choice in the same session, though the authors note this does not establish causal or temporal mediation.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings add to early evidence that simple behavioural training — practising non-response to certain foods — may shift the subjective appeal of those foods, with detectable brain-level correlates, which could have implications for understanding appetite regulation.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=85), women only, single-center, short follow-up, same-session mediation analysis (cannot establish temporal mediation), study conducted in China. Only 85 women studied, all from a single Chinese university, so results may not generalise to men or other populations; follow-up was same-session only so durability of the effect is unknown; mediation analysis cannot establish causality *Editor's fact-check note: N=85 confirmed from abstract. studies.headline: Just looking at a disgusting image is enough to slow your stomach's natural rhythm
studies.summary: Researchers at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev recorded the stomach's electrical activity in 46 participants (mostly female undergraduate students) while they viewed appetising, disgusting, or neutral images for about 13 minutes each. studies.why_it_matters: The finding that emotions triggered purely by vision can modulate stomach rhythms suggests a concrete physiological pathway linking psychological states and digestive function, which may be relevant to understanding conditions like nausea, appetite dysregulation, and gut-brain disorders.

studies.headline: LGBTQ+ people in Malaysia distrust their institutions most when they fear being scapegoated — and women and non-binary people feel it hardest
studies.summary: Using a mixed-methods design, researchers surveyed 647 LGBTQ+ adults in Malaysia about their trust in police, political, legal, and media institutions, and analysed open-ended responses from 228 participants. They found that cisgender women, trans men, and non-binary participants reported higher institutional distrust than cisgender men, as did Malay and Indian participants compared to Chinese participants. Qualitative analysis identified three drivers of distrust: being scapegoated, fear of dehumanisation, and diminishing hope for the future.
studies.why_it_matters: The study shows that institutional distrust among LGBTQ+ people in contexts of legal discrimination is not uniform — gender identity and ethnicity intersect to shape who feels most endangered, with implications for mental health and healthcare access in similar environments worldwide.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, small qualitative subsample (N=228 for qualitative component). Observational and self-reported; findings are specific to Malaysia's legal and cultural context and may not generalise; the qualitative sample is a subset of the survey sample; no causal claims can be made *Editor's fact-check note: The qualitative subsample is N=228, not the full N=647; this distinction has been accurately reflected in the summary.*

studies.headline: Scientists can now read the melody playing in your head directly from brain signals
studies.summary: Researchers recorded intracranial brain activity (electrocorticography, ECoG) from 10 epilepsy patients (3 male, 7 female; mean age 27.3) while they imagined familiar melodies presented in different musical keys. Using a relative-pitch decoding framework — focusing on intervals between notes rather than absolute pitch — machine-learning models could reconstruct melodic contours from neural signals at above-chance accuracy. While single-note decoding was modest, sequentially integrating decoded notes preserved the recognisable structure of the imagined melody, providing a proof-of-concept that internally generated music can be partially read from brain recordings.
studies.why_it_matters: Decoding internally imagined sound could one day help restore communication for people who can hear internally but cannot speak, and sheds light on how the brain constructs subjective auditory experience.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, participants were epilepsy patients (atypical brain organisation possible), invasive recording method limits generalisability. Decoding accuracy at the single-note level was modest; the technology is far from reading complete songs on demand

studies.headline: College students say collective trauma — mass shootings and war — hits harder than personal loss
studies.journal: Psychological Trauma: Theory, Research, Practice and Policy
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed racially diverse first- and third-year college students in the American Southeast (Study 1: N=165, Study 2: N=98) asking them to describe their past-year traumatic experiences in open-ended responses. Collective trauma — events experienced through the broader community, such as exposure to school or mass shootings and international conflicts like the Israel-Hamas/Gaza war — was the most commonly reported category, accounting for roughly half of all trauma descriptions in both samples. Students frequently reported learning about these collective traumas via social media, suggesting digital media plays a key role in how young people are now exposed to traumatic events.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that rising rates of anxiety and depression among college students may be partly driven by shared, media-mediated collective traumas rather than only individual life experiences — with implications for how universities design mental health support.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, geographically limited (American Southeast). Both samples drawn from universities in the American Southeast, limiting generalisability; self-reported and qualitative; does not measure clinical outcomes or diagnose PTSD; cross-sectional snapshot of a single academic year *Editor's fact-check note: Study 1 N=165, Study 2 N=98 — confirmed from abstract. Combined total is 263, not a single sample. Confirmed collective trauma was most common category (49.1–52.0%) across both studies. Noted geographic limitation (American Southeast) in caveats.*

studies.headline: Parents of children with severe epilepsy find hope — not regret — in clinical trials, even when they don't work
studies.summary: Researchers conducted the first cross-sectional survey exploring how caregivers perceived their child's participation in randomised controlled trials for Dravet syndrome, a severe childhood epilepsy. Forty-four caregivers (across four trials testing stiripentol, cannabidiol, fenfluramine, and soticlestat conducted between 1996 and 2024) completed a semi-structured questionnaire in French. The survey found that overall trial experiences were rated positively — hope was the dominant emotion throughout — and that feelings of regret and post-trial solitude were scored very low. The main barriers were logistical, relating to fitting frequent medical appointments around daily schedules.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding what motivates families to enrol in — and what puts them off — rare-disease trials could help researchers design more caregiver-friendly studies and improve recruitment for future clinical research in paediatric epilepsy.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, short follow-up. Very small sample (N=44), self-reported and retrospective data, survey conducted in French only (likely French-speaking families), no comparison group of caregivers who declined participation, and results may reflect selection bias toward families already positively disposed to research *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract notes N=44 total caregiver responses across four trials (10 STP, 20 CBD, 13 FFA, 1 TAK-935). studies.headline: How you stress a sentence is a personal signature — listeners can't change it
studies.summary: Researchers at the University of Potsdam tested whether 30 adult native German speakers (mean age 24.2) would alter their use of prosodic boundary cues — pitch range, pause duration, and syllable lengthening — when a listener appeared to misunderstand them. Despite receiving feedback indicating confusion, speakers maintained their individual, consistent patterns of prosodic cuing rather than shifting to a clearer speaking style, suggesting that how people mark phrase boundaries in speech reflects an internal, speaker-driven process rather than an adaptive response to the listener.
studies.why_it_matters: These findings suggest that core aspects of how we structure spoken language may be less socially flexible than assumed, which has implications for understanding communication breakdowns and potentially for speech therapy and human-computer interaction design.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=30), single-center, study conducted in German speakers only (University of Potsdam), lab-based confederate interaction rather than naturalistic communication. Only 30 German speakers were tested in a single lab using a scripted confederate, so results may not generalise to other languages, older populations, or real-world conversation. The confederate's misunderstandings were pre-programmed, not genuine *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirmed N=30, mean age 24.2, German speakers. Finding direction confirmed: speakers showed intra-individual stability despite listener feedback. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: More than half of high-risk pregnant women show signs of depression — and feeling out of control makes it worse
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed 327 women with high-risk pregnancies hospitalised in a tertiary centre in Central Anatolia, Turkey, using standardised self-report tools. They found that 57.8% showed elevated depressive symptoms and 43.7% showed elevated anxiety symptoms. Psychological symptoms — including prenatal distress and negative pregnancy perception — were the strongest predictors of poor mental health outcomes, outweighing sociodemographic factors in hierarchical regression analysis.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that routine mental health screening and psychosocial support should be integrated into high-risk obstetric care, as psychological vulnerability appears to compound the clinical stressors already present in these pregnancies.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Single hospital in Turkey limits generalisability; all outcomes are self-reported; observational design means causality cannot be established

studies.headline: Mental and physical exhaustion together hit soldiers' shooting accuracy far harder than either alone
studies.summary: Researchers had 24 military personnel (mean age 22, 20 male) complete three separate sessions inducing physical fatigue, cognitive fatigue, or both simultaneously, then measured marksmanship accuracy, reaction time, and efficiency. Combined fatigue produced significantly greater performance decrements than either type alone (Cohen's d = 0.78–1.12), with accuracy differences reaching large effect sizes (partial η² = 0.57). Participants also reported higher mental demand, temporal pressure, and frustration under combined conditions, suggesting the two fatigue types compound rather than simply add together.
studies.why_it_matters: Most military training and operational planning treats physical and mental exhaustion as separate concerns; this study suggests their simultaneous occurrence creates a qualitatively worse performance problem that may need dedicated countermeasures.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, predominantly male sample, self-reported outcomes (workload scales). Only 24 participants, almost all male, in a controlled lab setting — real combat involves many other variables. Self-reported workload measures are subjective. Results may not transfer to civilian or female populations

studies.headline: Depression in young Sāmoan women often masks years of hidden childhood sexual abuse, practitioners say
studies.summary: Researchers conducted talanoa (culturally grounded dialogue) interviews with 16 mental health practitioners in Aotearoa New Zealand who work with young Sāmoan women aged 18–24 presenting with depression. A consistent pattern emerged: depression frequently conceals long-silenced experiences of child sexual abuse (CSA), with disclosures typically surfacing only after several years. Practitioners reported identifying trauma through relational, culturally attuned engagement rather than direct disclosure, pointing to cultural and familial norms that restrict conversations about sexual harm in Sāmoan communities.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that standard depression assessments may systematically miss hidden trauma in Sāmoan and Pacific women, reinforcing the case for trauma-informed, culturally grounded mental health care for minoritised populations.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), qualitative/observational design, single-center, practitioner-reported (not survivor-reported) outcomes. studies.headline: Children's visual-motor skills plateau after third grade, not continue improving
studies.summary: Researchers assessed visual-motor integration skills — the ability to coordinate what the eyes see with hand movements — in 270 Turkish primary school children (Grades 1–4) using shape-copying and symmetry-completion tasks. ANOVA analyses found that visuomotor accuracy improved significantly up to Grade 3 but then plateaued in Grade 4. Children also performed consistently better on symmetry completion than on shape copying, suggesting the two tasks tap different cognitive and motor processes.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding when visual-motor development naturally plateaus could help educators and clinicians identify children who fall behind at a critical window, informing earlier screening in primary schools.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 per grade group), single-center, observational design, narrow regional sample (Turkey). Single-country sample (Turkey), observational design, subgroup sizes per grade are small, and rubric-based scoring introduces some subjectivity *Editor's fact-check note: Total N is 270, which is above 100 overall, but subgroup sizes per grade are not specified and likely below 100 each; flagged accordingly. Study is conducted in Turkey — findings may not generalize to other educational systems.*

studies.headline: For Gaelic Games athletes, resilience protects mental health — but the type of resilience matters depending on what's burning them out
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed 225 Gaelic Games athletes in Ireland using online self-report measures of burnout, depressive symptoms, somatic symptoms, and resilience (personal and relational). Using structural equation modelling, they found that relational resilience — such as peer support — mediated the link between emotional and physical exhaustion and depressive symptoms, while personal resilience — such as psychological skills — mediated the link between a reduced sense of accomplishment and somatic (physical) symptoms. The findings suggest that different types of resilience protect against different mental health outcomes in athlete burnout.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that no single resilience-building strategy fits all burnout pathways challenges one-size-fits-all athlete wellbeing programmes, suggesting sport organisations may need to tailor mental health support to the specific form of burnout athletes are experiencing.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single sport/cultural context (Gaelic Games, Ireland). Cross-sectional survey design means causation cannot be established; all measures are self-reported; findings come from a specific Irish amateur-sport context that may not generalise to professional or non-Gaelic-sport settings *Editor's fact-check note: N=225 confirmed in abstract. Study is observational cross-sectional (online survey), not longitudinal, which is a caveat not immediately obvious from headline framing — noted. No industry funding declared.*

studies.headline: Negative thinking traps the mind in a self-reinforcing loop — and rumination is the key driver
studies.summary: Researchers from Tilburg University and KU Leuven followed 179 adults with varying levels of depression and social anxiety over 14 days using ecological momentary assessment (12,950 completed surveys), asking them to complete a novel mobile cognitive task measuring how rigidly they held negative interpretations of ambiguous situations, alongside self-reported rumination and positive-emotion dampening. Multilevel and dynamic structural equation analyses found that when people became more locked into negative interpretations momentarily, they were more likely to ruminate and dampen positive emotions shortly after — and rumination (but not dampening) in turn increased negative interpretation inflexibility. These reciprocal effects were not stronger in people with higher depression or anxiety.
studies.why_it_matters: Pinpointing negative interpretation inflexibility as both a cause and consequence of rumination in everyday life suggests it could be a specific target for just-in-time digital interventions aimed at breaking harmful thought cycles.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, community sample may not generalise to clinical populations. Observational EMA design cannot establish causation; self-reported rumination and dampening; community sample skews away from severe clinical presentations; effect sizes for some cross-lagged links are small

studies.headline: Teens most prone to depression online are also the easiest to pull back from the brink
studies.summary: Researchers tracked 4,181 Chinese adolescents (57.5% female, mean age 15.4 years) at baseline, with 2,705 providing follow-up data one year later, to examine how profiles of co-occurring problematic internet use and depressive symptoms changed over time. Four distinct profiles were identified — low-risk, depressive-dominant, internet-use-dominant, and high-risk co-occurring — and transitions between these profiles were linked to motivational and self-regulatory brain systems. Counterintuitively, the depressive-dominant profile showed the highest rate of natural improvement over the year, while a heightened behavioural inhibition system predicted entry into symptomatic profiles and stronger self-control and emotion regulation predicted recovery.
studies.why_it_matters: Identifying which adolescents are most likely to improve without intervention — and which brain-system factors predict that recovery — could help focus limited mental health resources on teens at highest risk of staying stuck.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, sample from China only (findings may not generalise globally). studies.headline: Stress hormone that raises risk-taking in soldiers is not the one scientists expected
studies.summary: Researchers pharmacologically stimulated noradrenaline and/or cortisol activity in 100 Dutch military personnel using yohimbine and hydrocortisone, then assessed working memory, impulse control, and risk-taking via computerised tasks. They found that noradrenaline — not cortisol — drove increased risk-taking, contrasting prior research in civilians that implicated cortisol. Noradrenaline also slowed working-memory recall while cortisol accelerated it, and neither hormone affected impulse control.
studies.why_it_matters: Military personnel routinely make high-stakes decisions under acute stress, and identifying which specific stress chemicals drive risk-taking — rather than treating stress hormones as interchangeable — could inform future research on decision-making resilience in demanding occupations.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=100), single-center, single country/military subgroup (Dutch military), pharmacological induction may not fully replicate real-world stress. studies.headline: Babies' sense of vocal agency develops differently depending on their culture
studies.summary: Researchers used the still-face paradigm — where a caregiver suddenly becomes unresponsive — to test whether infants increase vocalising when ignored, taken as a sign of emerging vocal agency. Contrary to predictions, 4.5-month-old infants in neither culture yet showed a robust 'vocal extinction burst,' but German infants vocalised significantly more overall and showed longer vocalisations during the still-face episode, suggesting cultural parenting style shapes the pace at which vocal agency emerges.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that developmental milestones in early communication are not universal but are shaped by cultural caregiving practices, which has implications for how researchers and clinicians interpret infant vocal development across diverse populations.

studies.headline: Women of reproductive age face higher risk of skin reactions from common epilepsy drug
studies.summary: Researchers at Hiroshima University examined records from 3,379 epilepsy patients (49.3% women, mean age 38.2 years) who started lamotrigine (LTG) or levetiracetam (LEV) between 2008 and 2024. They found that cutaneous adverse drug reactions (skin rashes) to LTG were more than twice as likely in women as in men (odds ratio 2.44), with risk rising across the premenopausal period and dropping sharply after menopause. LEV showed a much more favourable safety profile, with skin reactions occurring in only 0.086% of users regardless of sex or age.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that reproductive hormonal status — not just drug dose — may influence a patient's likelihood of developing skin reactions to one of the world's most commonly prescribed epilepsy medications, potentially informing how clinicians counsel women of reproductive age who are starting this treatment.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center. Single-centre study from Japan, so rates may not generalise globally; retrospective observational design cannot establish causation; the role of hormonal contraception was not fully analysed and requires prospective investigation *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=3,379, single center (Hiroshima University Hospital), retrospective observational design. LTG CADR frequency confirmed at 3.2% (n=33) with six severe cases (0.58%). LEV CADR rate confirmed at 0.086%. No pregnancy-period CADRs among 63 childbirth events confirmed. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: People with bipolar disorder choose different suicide methods at different ages — and the pattern is distinct from the general population
studies.summary: Using Taiwan's nationwide health database, researchers tracked 47,488 individuals with bipolar disorder between 2003 and 2023, identifying 1,452 suicide deaths over 478,729 person-years. Compared with 81,159 general-population suicide decedents, those with bipolar disorder were significantly more likely to die by drowning (aOR 1.70) and jumping from height (aOR 1.31), but less likely to use hanging or charcoal burning. Age-stratified analyses revealed that method preferences shifted across the lifespan, with drowning elevated at all ages and jumping more common in middle-aged and older decedents.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding that suicide method selection in bipolar disorder follows distinct, age-dependent patterns could help clinicians and public health planners tailor prevention strategies — such as means restriction — more precisely to specific risk groups.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-country (Taiwan) data. Data from Taiwan only; some method patterns (charcoal burning) are culturally specific; observational design means causation cannot be inferred; decedent-only design limits ability to examine broader risk factors *Editor's fact-check note: The study population is Taiwan-specific; method patterns (e.g. charcoal burning prevalence) reflect cultural and geographic context that may not generalise globally. Noted in caveats_to_flag rather than triggering exclusion, as the underlying biological and clinical mechanisms of bipolar-related suicide risk have clear universal relevance.*

studies.headline: Competing against someone makes you faster but worse at holding back — and your brain shows why
studies.summary: Researchers at Nanjing University recruited 43 participants to complete a Go/NoGo task — requiring rapid responses to some stimuli and deliberate restraint to others — under both a social-competition condition and a control condition, while EEG recorded their brain activity. Social competition made participants respond faster without sacrificing accuracy on 'go' trials, but it also caused more errors on 'no-go' trials where they were supposed to withhold a response. EEG data showed that competition amplified a brain signal (the P3 component) linked to response preparation, and this neural change statistically explained both the speed boost and the increase in impulsive errors.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that social competition simultaneously sharpens and destabilises self-control at the neural level — a tension with implications for understanding behaviour in high-stakes competitive environments such as sports, exams, trading floors, and online gaming.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design. Direction of effects confirmed: faster Go RTs, more NoGo commission errors, enhanced P3 amplitudes under competition. No preregistration noted in abstract. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: When women start and stop HRT shapes the physical structure of their brains, genetic study suggests
studies.summary: Using Mendelian randomisation and double machine learning applied to UK Biobank neuroimaging data covering 1,366 brain imaging phenotypes, researchers examined whether the timing and lifetime use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) causally affects brain structure in women. They found that later initiation of HRT was associated with lower white-matter organisation in the right cerebellum, later cessation was linked to differences in cortical thickness and surface area, and ever-use of HRT was associated with larger volumes in the right inferior frontal gyrus and nucleus accumbens. Results were FDR-corrected and independently validated but require replication in external neuroimaging cohorts.
studies.why_it_matters: As millions of women navigate decisions about HRT timing during menopause, genetic-instrument evidence suggesting that when therapy starts and stops — not just whether it is used — may shape brain structure adds an important new dimension to ongoing debates about hormone therapy and brain ageing.
studies.caveats: observational design (MR cannot fully exclude pleiotropy), UK Biobank population (predominantly European ancestry), no direct cognitive or clinical outcome measured, requires external replication. Mendelian randomisation is not a clinical trial and cannot fully rule out confounding via pleiotropy; sample is predominantly European ancestry from UK Biobank; no direct memory or cognitive outcomes were measured; findings need replication in independent neuroimaging datasets *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract notes one secondary association (left tapetum FA) was excluded from primary conclusions due to significant directional pleiotropy — this is correctly reflected in the summary by focusing on primary findings only. Sample size for the neuroimaging cohort is not explicitly stated in the abstract beyond '1366 brain imaging-derived phenotypes'; N for participants is drawn from UK Biobank but not specified numerically in the abstract, so exact N is not quoted.*

studies.headline: Women with sexual abuse histories are twice as likely to drink alcohol to cope with sex-related distress

studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that sexual victimization history shapes the overlapping motivations behind both sexual behavior and alcohol use in women, pointing to a need for interventions that address these two risk factors together rather than in isolation.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center (multi-institutional but US-only convenience sample). studies.headline: Your genes set the stage for mental illness — but your life writes the script
studies.summary: A theoretical framework paper by a researcher at Italy's Istituto Superiore di Sanità proposes distinguishing two types of causality in mental health: 'permissive' causality (factors that widen or narrow what outcomes are possible, such as genes and brain biology) and 'instructive' causality (factors that steer which specific outcome actually occurs, such as life events and personal context). The author argues that biological substrates like genes and brain regions only ever operate permissively — opening or closing a space of possibilities — while environmental and contextual factors can additionally be instructive, actively directing mental states toward specific trajectories. The framework has no original empirical data; it is a conceptual synthesis aimed at reframing how psychiatry designs treatments, particularly plasticity-enhancing therapies like antidepressants and psychedelics.
studies.why_it_matters: If biology only sets the range of possible mental states rather than determining outcomes, it reframes the role of therapy and social environment in mental health treatment — and offers a theoretical rationale for why the same drug works differently depending on life context.
studies.caveats: No empirical data — theoretical/conceptual paper only; single author; no peer-reviewed empirical validation presented. This is a theoretical opinion piece with no new empirical data; the framework has yet to be tested in clinical or experimental research; single-author perspective from one institution *Editor's fact-check note: Clarified that this is a theoretical framework with no original study participants or empirical dataset; summary adjusted to reflect this.*

studies.headline: Most children with epilepsy have at least one other major health condition — and it's often unrecognised

studies.headline: Hostile immigration policies erode children's mental health advantage — even for US-born Asian kids
studies.summary: Using data from the 2023 National Survey of Children's Health (a large, nationally representative US dataset) and the 2022 Immigration Policy Climate index, researchers at Rutgers University examined whether state-level immigration policy hostility was associated with changes in child mental health among children with immigrant versus US-born parents. studies.headline: IQ gains across generations don't reflect rising general intelligence — and the pattern is messier than anyone thought
studies.summary: Researchers analysed longitudinal cognitive ability data collected prospectively from 1957 to 1999, examining IQ test scores of 1,187 children and adolescents aged 7–15 years (89% White, 9% Black, 52% female) across three versions of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children. They investigated whether the Flynn Effect — the well-documented rise in mean IQ scores across generations — reflects gains in general cognitive ability (g) or is concentrated in specific domains. The study found clear evidence of the Flynn Effect but showed that gains varied substantially across cognitive domains and subtests, with no discernible pattern tied to how strongly each subtest measures g; performance IQ gains were larger than their g-loadings would predict, while verbal gains were smaller than expected.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings challenge the popular interpretation that rising IQ scores mean societies are getting broadly smarter, suggesting instead that something more specific — and still poorly understood — is driving generational cognitive shifts.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, sample skewed demographically (89% White). The cohort is described as 89% White and 9% Black, which is a demographic limitation worth flagging. Direction of effects confirmed: performance IQ gains exceeded verbal IQ gains in test-version analyses but the pattern reversed in cohort-based analyses, and subtest g-loading did not predict Flynn Effect magnitude. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: A chatbot halved performance anxiety in singing students — but couldn't help them become more expressive

studies.headline: It's not the mystical experience that helps MDMA therapy work — it's the good mood

studies.headline: Your brain actively blocks out distractions — it doesn't just passively ignore them
studies.summary: Researchers at Washington University in St. Louis conducted four experiments with human participants to test how the brain avoids salient but irrelevant distractors during visual search tasks. By manipulating how serially (one-by-one) participants searched for targets, they measured whether distractor avoidance changed with search strategy. Contrary to the 'attentional window' account — which holds that distractors are passively filtered out when attention is narrowly focused — they found that the strength of distractor avoidance did not change as a function of search seriality, suggesting the brain uses active, goal-driven top-down control to suppress distractions.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding that distraction suppression is an active cognitive process rather than a structural filter has implications for research into attention disorders and for designing environments that reduce unwanted cognitive interruption.
studies.caveats: None identified. Laboratory visual-search tasks may not fully represent real-world distraction; total participant N not reported in abstract and should be confirmed; experiments were not pre-registered *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not report total N for the experiments; sample size cannot be verified from the abstract alone. I have not specified N in the summary as it was not available. This should be confirmed from the full paper before publication.*

studies.headline: How fast you walk — and how often you step — predicts your brain's executive power in older age
studies.summary: Researchers at Ohio State University tested multiple measures of mobility and cognitive performance in 223 community-dwelling adults aged 18–85. Among adults aged 55 and older, both stride velocity and cadence (step frequency) were independently associated with executive function — the mental skills used for planning, focus, and self-control — even after accounting for age and education. studies.why_it_matters: If step frequency is a separable marker of cognitive health in older adults, it could offer a simple, low-cost screening tool and a potential target for lifestyle interventions aimed at preserving mental sharpness with age.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, cross-sectional (no causal inference possible). Cross-sectional design means we cannot say whether slower cadence causes cognitive decline or vice versa, or whether a third factor (e.g. overall fitness) explains both.
