studies.headline: Having more social connections is linked to higher suicide risk in women — not lower
studies.summary: Using two waves of longitudinal data from the Seoul Young Adult Panel Survey (n = 8,953 person-years) collected during the COVID-19 pandemic (2021–2022), a South Korean sociologist examined whether social capital — access to support through family, friends, neighbours, and coworkers — was associated with suicide ideation. Correlated random effects models, controlling for individual covariates and unobserved time-invariant factors, found that greater social capital was significantly associated with increased probability of suicidal intent over time. Critically, this effect was only statistically significant among women, not men.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding challenges the long-held assumption that stronger social networks protect against suicide risk, suggesting that for women in particular, social ties can sometimes impose psychological costs rather than benefits — a distinction that could inform how mental health support is designed.
studies.caveats: observational design, single country (South Korea — pandemic-specific context and cultural gender norms may limit generalisability), self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis. Observational data cannot establish causation. The study was conducted in Seoul during the COVID-19 pandemic, and South Korean cultural norms around gender roles and social obligation may make results specific to that context. Self-reported suicidal ideation was used rather than clinical assessment. Journalist should avoid implying social connection is harmful in general *Editor's fact-check note: N reported as 8,953 person-years (two-wave longitudinal panel), not unique individuals — this is accurately reflected in summary. Study is set in Seoul, South Korea, during the COVID-19 pandemic; findings may be specific to that sociocultural and temporal context.*

studies.headline: Schizophrenia may disrupt the brain's waste-clearance system, not just its neurotransmitters
studies.journal: The World Journal of Biological Psychiatry
studies.summary: Australian researchers measured RNA expression levels across more than 17,000 genes in Brodmann's area 9 — the prefrontal cortex — from post-mortem brain tissue of 81 people with schizophrenia and 70 healthy controls. Of 47 genes showing altered expression, many were linked not to classic neurotransmitter pathways but to water homeostasis, waste clearance, potassium buffering, and CSF circulation. studies.why_it_matters: If confirmed, the finding points toward entirely new drug targets in schizophrenia beyond the dopamine and glutamate systems that have dominated treatment for decades, potentially opening fresh avenues for a disorder where many patients respond poorly to existing medications.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, short follow-up. studies.headline: One in three Black women find childbirth traumatic — and a key screening tool now works for them
studies.summary: Researchers at Emory University tested the City Birth Trauma Scale (BiTS) — a measure of birth-related PTSD symptoms — in 130 Black postpartum women who were 6–8 weeks after delivery and had experienced trauma exposure. The scale showed excellent internal consistency and strong validity, with confirmatory factor analysis supporting a two-factor structure (birth-specific and general symptoms). One third (33.6%) of women reported their birth as traumatic; 4.6% met full DSM-5 criteria for PTSD and 7.6% exceeded the probable-PTSD threshold on the BiTS.
studies.why_it_matters: Black women in the US face disproportionately high rates of obstetric complications, yet birth-trauma screening tools had not previously been validated in this population — a gap this study begins to close, with implications for postpartum mental health equity.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100 is not applicable here — N=130), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes. Single US academic centre (Emory, Atlanta) limits generalisability; cross-sectional design assessed women at 6–8 weeks postpartum only; self-reported measures; PTSD prevalence estimates differ between BiTS cut-off (7.6%) and full DSM-5 criteria (4.6%) — journalists should note this distinction *Editor's fact-check note: N=130 exceeds the small-sample threshold so 'small sample' flag removed from caveats. studies.headline: Feeling good and feeling bad really are opposites, large dataset confirms
studies.summary: Researchers introduced openESM, an open-access database pooling 60 experience-sampling datasets from more than 16,000 participants and over 740,000 real-life observations collected via mobile devices. As a demonstration of the database's power, they analysed within-person correlations between positive and negative affect across 39 datasets, finding a large negative correlation of −0.49 (95% CI: −0.54 to −0.42), suggesting that in daily life, positive and negative emotions strongly pull in opposite directions within individuals. The database is freely searchable and downloadable via R and Python packages at openesmdata.org.
studies.why_it_matters: Pooling thousands of people's daily emotional experiences in one harmonised archive could resolve long-standing debates about how emotions are structured in everyday life, and give researchers the statistical power to answer questions no single study can.
studies.caveats: secondary analysis, observational design. This is primarily a methods/infrastructure paper; the emotion finding is a demonstration analysis using observational, self-reported mood data, so causal conclusions cannot be drawn. The correlation, while large, is a within-person average and may vary by population or context

studies.headline: Simulation training helps doctors learn seizure emergencies — but there is no proof it saves patients
studies.summary: A scoping review of 21 studies published between 2015 and 2025 synthesised evidence on simulation-based education for emergency management of status epilepticus, covering 1,425 trainees across eight countries. Eighty-one per cent of studies (17 of 21) found significant improvements in knowledge or procedural skills after simulation training, and team-based designs consistently improved task coordination. However, the review found almost no patient-level evidence: the single study that assessed actual clinical outcomes found no significant effect on patient care.
studies.why_it_matters: Status epilepticus is a life-threatening neurological emergency, and simulation training has become widespread — but this review suggests that improving clinician test scores does not automatically translate into better outcomes for real patients, a distinction that matters for how healthcare systems invest in training.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, self-reported outcomes, short follow-up. Scoping reviews do not pool statistics; this is a narrative synthesis of 21 mostly small, non-randomised studies with heterogeneous outcome measures. The review is concentrated in high-resource settings and may not reflect training challenges in lower-income countries. Patient-outcome evidence is almost entirely absent, making any causal claim about clinical impact impossible *Editor's fact-check note: N=1,425 refers to trainees across all included studies, not a single study sample; individual studies are characterised by small samples. Caveats reflect the limitations of included studies as described in the abstract. The review itself is a scoping review, not a meta-analysis.*

studies.headline: People with inflammatory bowel disease worry less about how their body looks and more about whether it will betray them in public
studies.summary: Australian researchers at Flinders University conducted co-design workshop interviews with 10 people living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD; 8 women, 2 men; mean age 35) and analysed the transcripts using reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: body image concerns tied to bodily function rather than appearance; the central role of eating and symptom control; and the pervasive anxiety around unpredictability and social visibility of symptoms. studies.headline: Fear of losing money focuses the mind almost as well as the promise of gaining it — but not quite
studies.summary: Researchers at the University of Chicago recruited 30 participants to complete a sustained attention task (continuous performance task) while varying the motivational stakes every 20 trials: potential reward, potential penalty, both combined, or no incentive. Replicating prior work, rewards reduced attentional lapses versus no incentive. Crucially, the threat of penalties also improved sustained attention — but the penalty-only condition was less effective than combining reward and penalty, and neither alone was compared directly in the abstract as superior to reward alone.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding whether carrots and sticks work differently on attention has practical implications for how workplaces, schools, and clinical settings structure motivation — and this study suggests that combining both types of incentive may be the most powerful approach for maintaining focus.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, laboratory task (limited ecological validity), study not preregistered. Very small sample of only 30 participants severely limits statistical power and generalisability; this is a controlled laboratory task that may not reflect real-world attention demands; the study was not preregistered; direct statistical comparison between reward-only and penalty-only conditions is not clearly reported in the abstract *Editor's fact-check note: N=30 confirmed from abstract. The abstract states penalty was less effective than the combined condition but does not explicitly state penalty was less effective than reward alone — only that the 'motivational mechanisms may differ depending on the type of benefit — particularly when avoiding penalties alone.' Headline and summary adjusted to reflect this nuance accurately.*

studies.headline: As the brain learns a new skill, it quietly stops trying so hard
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a systematic review of 23 EEG studies examining the brain's electrical activity during motor sequence learning — the process by which discrete movements become automatic skills. Across studies they found that learning is associated with reduced midline theta activity (suggesting less effortful top-down control), shifts in alpha-band rhythms linked to better movement prediction, and mixed beta-band changes tied to motor planning. Connectivity findings were limited but pointed to reduced functional coupling between brain regions as sequences become automatic.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding how the brain transitions from effortful to automatic movement could inform rehabilitation strategies for people relearning skills after stroke or brain injury, as well as training programmes for musicians, athletes, and surgeons.
studies.caveats: Review of 23 studies with substantial methodological heterogeneity, no meta-analysis, findings described as fragmented. This is a narrative review, not a new empirical study; the authors themselves note substantial methodological inconsistencies across the 23 papers reviewed. No causal claims should be made *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms a review of 23 studies; no empirical participant data is reported (this is a review/synthesis paper). Summary reflects this accurately.*

studies.headline: Gambling recovery isn't just about stopping — it ends in post-traumatic growth, study finds
studies.summary: Researchers in France used constructivist grounded theory to interview 20 people who self-identified as either recovered from or currently recovering from gambling disorder. Analysing semi-structured interviews, they identified nine distinct stages of recovery — from initially acknowledging a problem through to post-traumatic growth — suggesting recovery extends far beyond simply stopping gambling to involve identity reconstruction and meaning-making. Both groups described all nine stages, though their experiences differed by recovery status.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that gambling recovery can culminate in post-traumatic growth challenges purely abstinence-focused treatment models and suggests clinicians and support services may need to address identity and meaning alongside behaviour change.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, industry funding [FDJ and PMU via Nantes University Hospital Endowment Fund]. Only 20 participants in a single French centre; qualitative model not yet empirically validated; study was partly funded by gambling industry operators FDJ and PMU (though researchers assert independence); findings may not generalise across cultures or treatment systems *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=20 (10 recovered, 10 recovering), qualitative/grounded theory design, and industry funding from gambling operators FDJ and PMU — all reflected accurately above.*

studies.headline: Men gain less from campus sexual-violence prevention training than women — and the effects fade within months
studies.summary: A pilot study at US universities evaluated the Mentors in Violence Prevention (MVP) programme — a gender-transformative bystander education initiative — among student leaders in athletics, fraternities and sororities, and residential life. Using a single-group repeated-measures design without a control group, researchers measured activist attitudes and bystander intentions before training, immediately after, and three months later. The one-day programme produced significant short-term improvements in activist outcomes for both women and men, but effects waned by the three-month follow-up, women benefited more than men, and gender ideology interacted with peer-group membership to shape how much participants gained. The study does not report the precise total N in the abstract.
studies.why_it_matters: Campus sexual-violence prevention programmes are now widely mandated, yet this study suggests that single-day trainings may not produce lasting change — especially in the men they most aim to reach — raising questions about what dosage and format are actually needed.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, short follow-up, no control group. This is a pilot study with no control group, relying on self-reported attitudes rather than behaviour, conducted at US universities only — results may not generalise. The precise sample size is not stated in the abstract and should be confirmed before publication *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not specify a total participant N; 'small sample (N<100)' is flagged as likely given pilot study description, but cannot be confirmed from abstract text alone — journalist should verify with authors. studies.headline: A Canadian hospital is wrapping ketamine infusions inside full psychological support — and tracking whether it works

The paper is a methodological framework paper, not an outcomes study — no patient outcome data are yet reported. The program began formally in 2023, building on ketamine infusions offered at the hospital since 2010, and is prospectively collecting data on pain, sleep, psychological factors, and functioning for a future publication.
studies.why_it_matters: As ketamine use for both chronic pain and mental health conditions expands rapidly, this program description offers a model for how specialised psychological support could be systematically integrated into infusion protocols — a gap that critics of current ketamine clinics frequently flag.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, no outcome data reported yet (framework/methodology paper only). This paper describes a program framework only — no patient outcomes have been reported yet. Single hospital in Toronto; results when published will need scrutiny for selection bias and lack of a control group. Journalists should be careful not to imply the integrated model has already been shown to outperform standard ketamine infusion *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract explicitly states outcome data will be presented in a future article; this paper reports no efficacy findings. studies.headline: Combining breathing, brain, and heart training cuts reaction time better than any one technique alone
studies.summary: Researchers at Islamic Azad University in Tehran tested whether combining beta-theta neurofeedback, heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback, and box-breathing simultaneously would outperform either technique used alone. Twenty-two healthy university students (N=22; 6 male, 16 female) were randomly assigned to one of three groups across 10 sessions. The group receiving all three interventions together showed significantly faster visual-recognition reaction times than those who received only breathwork or only neurofeedback plus HRV biofeedback, alongside measurable changes in brainwave and heart rate markers.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that layering mind-body training techniques may produce additive cognitive benefits, with potential implications for performance training and attention-related research.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, healthy student population only, Iran-based single institution. Tiny sample of just 22 students, conducted at a single university in Tehran, all participants were healthy young adults — so findings cannot be extended to older adults, clinical populations, or different cultural contexts. No long-term follow-up, and it is unclear whether reaction-time gains persist after training ends *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=22 across three groups (N=7, N=8, N=7). Study conducted in Tehran, Iran with student participants; generalisability to broader populations is limited. No corrections needed to key facts.*

studies.headline: Your heartbeat shapes how much social rejection hurts — and this holds true even in older age
studies.summary: In a pre-registered study, younger and older adults played a computerised ball-tossing game (Cyberball) in which social exclusion events were timed to occur either during cardiac systole or diastole, allowing researchers to test whether the phase of the heartbeat modulates the emotional sting of being left out. Despite older adults showing measurably lower heart rate variability and reduced body awareness, both age groups reported less social pain when exclusion happened during systole than during diastole — replicating the effect previously seen only in younger adults. The study did not report a combined N in the abstract.
studies.why_it_matters: The result suggests that the body's internal signalling system — specifically the baroreceptor signals sent during each heartbeat — continues to buffer emotional pain well into older adulthood, even as other markers of interoception decline with age.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, sample size not reported in abstract. Social pain was self-reported via a game simulation, not real-world exclusion; the total sample size is not reported in the abstract; the study was conducted in Japan and findings should be replicated across cultures *Editor's fact-check note: The abstract does not state the total N; summary notes this rather than inventing a figure.*

studies.headline: Spaced deadlines don't actually stop procrastination, major replication finds
studies.summary: Researchers attempted to replicate Study 2 from the influential Ariely and Wertenbroch (2002) paper, which claimed that evenly spaced, externally imposed deadlines help people overcome procrastination and improve performance. In their replication with adult university students in the United States, changes in deadline spacing had a negligible effect on three performance metrics and several survey measures. The study found no evidence that evenly spaced externally imposed deadlines were particularly effective at reducing procrastination compared to other conditions.
studies.why_it_matters: The original finding has been widely cited to justify deadline-setting policies in education and workplaces; this failed replication suggests those recommendations may rest on shakier ground than previously assumed.
studies.caveats: single-center, observational design. Sample size not reported in abstract; single university setting; replication of one study does not definitively settle the question — other deadline research exists; participants were students, limiting generalisability to other populations *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract does not report a specific N for the replication sample; sample described only as 'adult participants enrolled at a large public university in the United States.' Could not verify N≥100 from abstract alone, so no N is stated in summary. No industry funding declared. Original study (Ariely & Wertenbroch) is cited as the source being replicated.*

studies.summary: In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial at the University of Zurich, 28 healthy male volunteers each received a combined harmine+DMT formulation (inspired by ayahuasca), harmine alone, or placebo. Compared with placebo, the harmine+DMT combination significantly reduced embarrassment specific to self-referential stimuli (one's own voice) and lowered overall experiential shame scores; harmine alone produced no significant effects.
studies.why_it_matters: Shame and embarrassment are core features of social anxiety, depression, and PTSD that current treatments address poorly; a targeted pharmacological approach to muting negative self-referential emotion could open a new treatment direction, though this was tested only in healthy men.

studies.headline: Dancing together doesn't just bond people — it quietly dismantles the social rules that keep groups apart
studies.summary: A researcher at Aarhus University and the Center for Mind and Culture synthesises evidence from cognitive motor science, biomusicology, and related fields to propose the 'Relaxed Priors through Synchrony' (RePS) model — a theoretical framework explaining how rhythmic interpersonal synchrony affects the brain's social processing. Rather than simply increasing group cohesion, the review argues that synchronised movement (such as dancing to shared music) reduces the brain's reliance on high-level social categories — such as ingroup/outgroup boundaries, status hierarchies, and roles — by boosting the precision of bottom-up sensorimotor signals relative to top-down social predictions. The author proposes this explains why synchrony reduces ingroup bias, rapidly bonds strangers, flattens hierarchies, and is associated with trance states — and why cultural authorities have historically suppressed expressive dance rather than championing it.
studies.why_it_matters: The model offers a novel cognitive account of why rhythm and dance occupy a central place in human rituals, weddings, and social transitions worldwide, and why authoritarian regimes and institutions have so often banned or stigmatised communal dancing.
studies.caveats: Theoretical/review paper, no original empirical data, single-author. This is a theoretical synthesis — no new data are presented, and the model awaits empirical testing. Single-author review without peer-reviewed empirical trials directly testing RePS claims. Journalist should present this as a compelling hypothesis, not established science *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms this is a theoretical review proposing a new model (RePS), not an empirical study. No participant N exists. Summary and caveats reflect this accurately.*

studies.headline: Inserting brain electrodes into epilepsy patients accidentally cuts their seizures in half — and no one knows why
studies.summary: Canadian researchers retrospectively analysed 51 adults with drug-resistant epilepsy who underwent stereoelectroencephalographic (SEEG) depth electrode implantation for diagnostic monitoring between December 2018 and February 2020. They found that simply inserting the electrodes — before any therapeutic intervention — reduced seizure frequency by 50% or more in 71% of patients at one month, with 43% achieving complete seizure freedom at that timepoint; effects partially persisted at 12 months (50% responder rate). No clinical or demographic factor — including age, sex, number of electrodes, or medication load — predicted who would respond.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that a diagnostic procedure alone can dramatically and durably reduce seizures in some of the hardest-to-treat epilepsy patients suggests that the physical act of electrode insertion may itself disrupt seizure-generating brain networks — an insight that could reshape how clinicians interpret surgical outcomes and think about therapeutic mechanisms.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, retrospective, short follow-up, incomplete medication tracking. Only 51 patients from a single Canadian centre; retrospective design means causality cannot be established; medication changes during the follow-up period were not fully tracked, which could partly explain the effect; effects waned over months for many patients *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=51, retrospective design, single centre (Western University, London, Ontario, Canada). studies.headline: Your brain can be trained to literally see the world differently — and the effect lasts
studies.summary: Researchers trained participants over 7 days on a visual task in which a target appeared at a fixed location alongside a competing distractor. Before and after training, they measured perceived contrast using psychophysical tests. Participants who trained under competition (N not specified per group, drawn from the full study) showed a lasting shift in how bright they perceived stimuli to be — locations that had competed for attention now appeared higher contrast with less physical light, while untrained locations required more light to appear equivalent. Training without distractors improved accuracy but did not change visual appearance.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that the visual brain does not simply learn to perform better — it may fundamentally recalibrate how physical reality is experienced, with implications for understanding how repeated attentional demands shape perception over time.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up. studies.headline: Overconfidence and loss aversion are not opposing flaws — they evolved to work together
studies.summary: Economists at the University of Bath and the London School of Economics developed a theoretical signalling model to explain why humans exhibit both overconfidence and loss aversion simultaneously — two biases long thought to work against each other. Their model proposes that overconfidence evolved as a credible signal of genuine ability (because more capable individuals bear lower costs from the errors it causes), while loss aversion evolved alongside it to privately dampen the decision-making costs overconfidence creates without undermining its social signalling function. This is a theoretical/computational study with no human participants.
studies.why_it_matters: The theory directly challenges Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman's influential prescription that people should try to eliminate both biases, suggesting instead that these traits may be adaptive when they operate together. It reframes apparent cognitive flaws as a coordinated evolved system.
studies.caveats: No human participants — theoretical/computational model only; no empirical primary data collected. This is a theoretical model, not an empirical study — no new human data were collected. The 'evidence' cited in support is drawn from existing literature. Journalists should be clear this is a theoretical framework that requires empirical testing, not a finding from a new experiment *Editor's fact-check note: This study presents a theoretical evolutionary signalling model with no primary human or animal data collection. studies.headline: Young adults say more about race in writing than in conversation with friends
studies.summary: Researchers recruited 107 friend-pairs (N = 214 total) of U.S. emerging adults who each wrote individual narratives about their racial/ethnic experiences and then had an unstructured conversation with their friend in which race/ethnicity came up. Qualitative analysis identified conversation dynamics — particularly encouragement versus mitigation — with encouragement associated with greater meaning-making.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that social context may suppress how deeply young people process racial experiences in real time, pointing to the potential value of structured or encouraging conversational environments for racial identity development.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center. studies.headline: Expensive brain mapping before epilepsy implants may not improve seizure outcomes
studies.summary: Researchers at the University of Utah retrospectively reviewed 99 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy who received responsive neurostimulation (RNS) implants between 2015 and 2024, comparing outcomes for those who did (N=78) versus did not (N=21) undergo prior stereo-electroencephalography (sEEG) brain mapping. Using propensity score matching to balance the groups, they found that preoperative sEEG monitoring was not associated with greater seizure reduction at last follow-up (overall mean reduction: 72.4%). The finding suggests that skipping the additional invasive mapping step does not appear to compromise outcomes for RNS candidates.
studies.why_it_matters: With epilepsy care delays worsening globally, evidence that a costly and invasive pre-surgical step may be skippable without reducing effectiveness could meaningfully streamline the treatment pathway for patients with uncontrolled seizures.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, retrospective, short matched group (N=21 per group). Retrospective single-centre study; matched groups of only 21 patients each; prospective trials needed before clinical practice changes; result does not establish that sEEG is never useful, only that it was not associated with better outcomes in this cohort *Editor's fact-check note: Total cohort is N=99 but propensity-matched groups are N=21 each; both figures are reported accurately from the abstract. studies.headline: Women's emotional distress during IVF follows three distinct patterns — and insomnia is one of the strongest warning signs
studies.summary: A prospective longitudinal study tracked psychological distress in 377 Chinese women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART) treatment across a complete clinical cycle. Using latent class growth modelling, researchers identified three distinct distress trajectories: stable-low, moderate-increasing, and high-acute. Women at highest risk of severe distress were more likely to have fewer viable embryos, higher insomnia severity, experience hostile social attitudes toward infertility, and face conflicts between work schedules and treatment appointments.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that distress during fertility treatment is not uniform and that modifiable factors — particularly sleep problems and workplace inflexibility — may flag women who need early psychological support. This points toward the need for routine longitudinal screening rather than one-off assessments during ART cycles.
studies.caveats: single-center, self-reported outcomes, observational design, study population limited to Chinese women at one hospital (findings tied to specific cultural attitudes toward infertility in China). All participants were recruited at a single Chinese hospital; cultural context — particularly social stigma around infertility — may differ significantly in Western settings. Self-reported measures and observational design mean causality cannot be established. Journalists should note the limited generalisability and avoid implying clinical action

studies.headline: We all look at the same things first — then our eyes go their own way
studies.summary: Researchers from the Medical Research Foundation in Chennai and Erasmus Medical Centre tracked the eye movements of 45 healthy adults (median age 38) as they freely viewed ten real-world scenes for 15 seconds each. During the first 7.5 seconds, gaze patterns were highly similar across participants and heavily guided by low-level visual salience (72% of fixations landing on model-predicted salient regions); in the second 7.5 seconds, viewing became increasingly individualised as higher-level, top-down cognitive factors took over. Scenes containing social elements attracted fewer purely salience-driven fixations throughout.
studies.why_it_matters: Understanding how attention shifts from automatic to personalised within seconds of seeing a scene has implications for designing assessments of visual and cognitive function, including potential tools for detecting conditions such as autism, ADHD, or dementia in which this balance may be altered.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design, used a single computational saliency model (Itti & Koch) that may not capture all bottom-up features. Only 45 participants; single-centre; saliency measured with one older computational model; causality cannot be established; clinical applications remain speculative *Editor's fact-check note: N=45 confirmed; median age and IQR figures match abstract. The 72% median saliency-directed fixation figure is for the early phase specifically, as stated in the abstract — correctly represented in summary.*

studies.headline: Long-term antipsychotic use rewires the brain's motor circuits — and the damage may be irreversible
studies.summary: Researchers from institutions in India conducted a narrative review integrating molecular, structural, and clinical evidence on tardive dyskinesia (TD) — a potentially permanent movement disorder caused by chronic antipsychotic use. The review proposes that TD is not simply a result of dopamine receptor supersensitivity, but rather the endpoint of cascading neurobiological adaptations including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress signalling, and multi-neurotransmitter dysregulation that progressively destabilise motor circuits. studies.why_it_matters: Antipsychotics are prescribed to millions of people with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and other conditions; reframing tardive dyskinesia as a disorder of pathological neuroplasticity — rather than a simple pharmacological side effect — could reshape how psychiatrists monitor and minimise this risk.
studies.caveats: narrative (non-systematic) review, no original human data, preclinical and clinical evidence synthesised without meta-analytic rigour *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract is a narrative review with no participant sample. No N applicable. Caveats reflect review methodology.*

studies.headline: Women feel heat pain sooner than men, but only at low intensities
studies.summary: Researchers exposed 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women to contact heat stimuli at three temperatures (42, 46, and 50°C) applied to the thigh, measuring how quickly each sex reported warmth, heat, and pain sensations. At near-threshold heat (42°C), women reported the onset of pain roughly 40% sooner than men (110 s vs. 180 s), but this sex difference disappeared at higher temperatures. Sensations of warmth and general heat did not differ between sexes at any intensity.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding suggests that sex-based differences in pain sensitivity are intensity-dependent rather than uniform, which could influence how pain thresholds are assessed in clinical and occupational settings.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, study population from South Korea. Only 16 participants total (8 per sex), conducted at a single centre in South Korea, so results need replication in larger and more diverse samples before any clinical conclusions can be drawn

studies.headline: Hot nights are stealing up to 17 minutes of sleep per person — and the poor lose more
studies.summary: Researchers analysed approximately 165 million nights of sleep tracker data from 317,758 users of Withings devices across the globe, collected between January 2020 and September 2023. Using a case-time-series design, they linked each night's sleep duration to local ambient temperature. At high temperatures (99th versus 50th percentile of the global distribution; 27.3°C vs 12.2°C), participants lost roughly 15–17 minutes of sleep per night and were approximately 40% more likely to sleep fewer than six hours. People in lower-GDP countries and older adults suffered the greatest losses.
studies.why_it_matters: As climate change pushes average temperatures higher, these findings suggest sleep deprivation could become an amplifier of existing global health inequalities, disproportionately affecting populations least able to afford air conditioning or adapt their environments. The scale of the dataset makes this one of the most robust estimates of temperature's impact on sleep to date.
studies.caveats: self-reported outcomes, observational design. Sleep was measured by consumer wearables, not polysomnography, so accuracy varies; the dataset skews toward wealthier users who own sleep trackers, potentially underestimating effects in the poorest populations; observational design means causation cannot be confirmed, though the within-person case-time-series design strengthens the inference *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=317,758 and ~165 million nights. Sleep duration was measured by wearable/under-mattress devices rather than self-report in the traditional sense, though device accuracy varies; 'self-reported outcomes' flag is noted as the location data relied on user registration. studies.headline: Simple jury instructions could stop witnesses' changed stories from sending innocent people to prison
studies.summary: Researchers at UC San Diego used mock-trial transcripts to study how jurors respond when a witness first rejects a suspect in a police lineup but later confidently identifies them in court. In Study 1 (N=45), mock jurors tended to explain the inconsistency by attributing it to stress rather than memory contamination. In Study 2 (N=289), specially designed 'reflector variable' jury instructions helped jurors properly weigh the initial lineup rejection as evidence of innocence — whereas standard instructions left jurors equally likely to convict regardless of the lineup outcome.
studies.why_it_matters: Witness misidentification is a leading cause of wrongful convictions; this study suggests a low-cost courtroom intervention — revised jury instructions — may help jurors give appropriate weight to the most reliable memory evidence, the first identification attempt.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100) for Study 1, observational design, self-reported outcomes, mock-trial methodology (not real jurors). Both studies used online mock jurors via Prolific reading transcripts rather than real jury deliberations; Study 1 sample was only 45 participants. Results may not fully replicate in live courtrooms with actual deliberation dynamics *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms Study 1 N=45 and Study 2 N=289; both use Prolific panels with mock-trial transcripts, not real jurors — flagged as limitation. Direction of effect confirmed: reflector variable instructions improved discrimination between guilt and innocence evidence.*

studies.headline: Teen secrets aren't just rebellion — daily diary study links what adolescents hide from mums to emotional detachment, not independence
studies.summary: Using a 21-day diary design with 208 adolescents (mean age 15, 57% female) in Hong Kong, researchers tracked daily fluctuations in how much teens disclosed or concealed information from their mothers, alongside their sense of functional autonomy and emotional detachment. studies.caveats: single-center, self-reported outcomes, observational design, sample limited to Hong Kong adolescents. studies.headline: Psychedelic researchers have been measuring the wrong thing for 60 years, critics argue
studies.summary: In a theoretical and historical critique, researchers from Queen's University argue that the concept of 'mysticism' used to explain why psychedelics work therapeutically is based on flawed mid-20th century scholarship. The authors call for renaming the MEQ the Psychedelic Experience Questionnaire (PEQ), arguing this better reflects Pahnke's own later thinking and removes a conceptual straitjacket on the research.
studies.why_it_matters: If the main measure used to explain therapeutic outcomes from psychedelics is built on a contested and religiously loaded concept, it suggests the entire explanatory framework for why these treatments work may need rethinking.

studies.headline: Online therapy improves quality of life in chronic fatigue patients even when it doesn't change how they think
studies.summary: Finnish researchers conducted a randomised controlled trial testing internet-delivered Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (iACT) combined with standard care versus standard care alone in 103 adults with persistent physical symptoms linked to indoor environments or chronic fatigue syndrome. studies.why_it_matters: Online ACT-based therapy may offer a scalable route to improving daily functioning for people with hard-to-treat persistent physical symptoms, though understanding why it works remains an open question that could lead to more targeted treatments.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=103), self-reported outcomes, single-center, short follow-up. studies.headline: Older adults who die by suicide are more likely to have seen a doctor recently — pointing to missed prevention windows
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a retrospective national case series examining coronial records of all 654 older adults (aged ≥60) who died by suicide in Ireland between 2015 and 2020, compared with 18–59-year-old suicide decedents. Older adults who died by suicide were more likely to have had recent GP contact, physical health conditions, acute pain, and loneliness than younger decedents. Single older males had the highest suicide rate of any group at 38.1 per 100,000, and suicide risk among older adults peaked in summer months.
studies.why_it_matters: The pattern of recent healthcare contact before death suggests that GP appointments represent a critical — and currently underused — opportunity to identify and support at-risk older adults, particularly those experiencing physical illness and loneliness.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center (Ireland only), retrospective design, region-specific (Ireland coronial system). Data are from Ireland only and the coronial system may capture cases differently than other countries; retrospective observational design cannot establish causation; the comparison group is also suicide decedents, not the general population, which limits some inferences about risk factors *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract confirms N=654 older adults, national Irish coronial data 2015–2020, and the finding of higher GP contact among older suicide decedents. The overall older-adult rate (12.0 per 100,000) was lower than the 18–59 group (17.5 per 100,000), though single older males had the highest rate (38.1 per 100,000). No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: Believing in lucky charms actually improves learning — but only for people who don't trust their own abilities
studies.summary: Spanish researchers ran two studies with secondary school students to examine how desire for control and superstitious belief interact to affect learning performance. In a cross-sectional study, students with a high desire for control outperformed those with a low desire on a computerised reinforcement-learning task. In a 2×2 factorial experiment, students were exposed to a fabricated documentary inducing superstitious beliefs; superstition boosted learning performance among low-desire-for-control students but slightly harmed it among high-desire-for-control students. The sample sizes are not reported in the abstract.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest superstition is not uniformly irrational or harmful — for people who feel low personal agency, external 'magical' structures may provide enough psychological order to free up cognitive resources for learning.
studies.caveats: small sample (size not reported in abstract), observational design (Study 1), single-center (Spain), self-reported outcomes (Study 1), experimental manipulation used a fabricated documentary (ecological validity uncertain). The direction of the superstition effect (beneficial for low-desire, slightly harmful for high-desire students) is as stated in the abstract. No other corrections needed.*

studies.headline: A simple six-question PTSD screener scores as well as the gold standard in military veterans
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a ROC analysis to establish validated cut-off scores for the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ) PTSD subscale in a large sample of Norwegian military veterans (N = 5,640). Using the well-established PCL-5 as a benchmark, they found that a sum score of 6 on the ITQ's six symptom items offered the best balance of sensitivity and specificity for clinical screening, while a score of 7 was more appropriate for research settings. The study suggests the ITQ can serve as a reliable, streamlined screener for probable PTSD in military populations.
studies.why_it_matters: Providing validated, easy-to-use cut-off scores for the ITQ could improve PTSD identification in military contexts where rapid, accurate screening is critical. It also helps bridge two of the most widely used PTSD instruments, potentially improving consistency across clinical and research settings globally.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center (Norwegian military population), secondary analysis. All participants were Norwegian military veterans, so findings may not directly generalise to other cultural or military contexts; the ITQ scores were validated against another self-report measure (PCL-5) rather than a clinical diagnostic interview, which limits how far conclusions about true PTSD diagnosis can be drawn

studies.headline: Food addiction in teenagers drives later reward-based eating, but doesn't directly cause weight gain, study finds
studies.summary: Researchers in eastern China tracked 2,054 young people (mean ages 13–14) across two time points in a longitudinal panel study, measuring food addiction symptoms, eating motives, lifestyle habits, and body composition including BMI, subcutaneous fat, and visceral fat. Using cross-lagged panel network analysis, they found that food addiction was strongly associated with weight-related measures — particularly visceral fat — in cross-sectional data, but showed no direct longitudinal paths to weight gain over time. Instead, food addiction predicted subsequent reward-based and emotionally driven eating motives, and showed a bidirectional relationship with mindful eating.
studies.why_it_matters: The finding that food addiction may influence weight indirectly — through eating motivation patterns rather than directly adding kilograms — suggests that interventions targeting mindful eating and reward-driven behaviour could be more effective than those focused purely on dietary restriction.
studies.caveats: observational design, single-center, self-reported outcomes, short follow-up, study population limited to eastern China (findings may not generalise to other cultural or dietary contexts), industry funding [Boehringer Ingelheim — co-author Potenza]. studies.headline: Posttraumatic growth shields women's body image after childhood adversity — but the same effect doesn't hold for men
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed 481 Chinese adults (230 men, 251 women) who had each experienced at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE), examining how posttraumatic growth (PTG) relates to body appreciation. Higher ACE scores were associated with lower body appreciation in both sexes, with stronger effects in women. Crucially, higher levels of PTG significantly buffered the negative link between ACEs and body appreciation among women across multiple ACE subtypes — but this protective effect was not found in men, suggesting the psychological pathway from childhood adversity to body image differs by gender.
studies.why_it_matters: Body dissatisfaction is a significant risk factor for eating disorders and depression; understanding that posttraumatic growth may buffer this risk — particularly in women — could inform trauma-informed approaches to body image interventions.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, cross-sectional (no longitudinal data), sample limited to Chinese adults who had experienced ACEs. studies.headline: People with psychotic disorders who die in fatal car crashes are often seen by a doctor just weeks before
studies.summary: Finnish researchers analysed nationwide register data on 94 drivers with psychotic disorders who died in fatal motor vehicle accidents between 1990 and 2011, comparing them to 146 matched controls without psychiatric disorders. Drivers with psychotic disorders were nearly six times more likely to die shortly after their last healthcare contact than controls (adjusted HR = 5.82). Strikingly, 70% had died within six months of their last care visit, and among those whose deaths were classified as suicide, the median time from last contact to death was just 29 days.

studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that alcohol use may not serve the affect-regulation function many people believe it does, even among those at highest risk — pointing toward the potential value of alternative emotion-regulation interventions for vulnerable populations.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up, observational design, sensitivity analyses yielded mixed/nonsignificant results for individual substances. studies.headline: A mysterious form of status epilepticus leaves patients in intensive care five times longer than the standard kind
studies.summary: Researchers retrospectively compared 81 adults with refractory status epilepticus (RSE) admitted to two London hospitals between 2007 and 2023, splitting them into 29 with NORSE (new onset refractory status epilepticus, with no prior epilepsy history) and 52 with standard RSE. NORSE patients had dramatically longer intensive care stays (median 51 vs 11 days), needed more anti-seizure medications, and were significantly more likely to leave hospital with cognitive impairment (89% vs 62%). Surprisingly, six-month mortality was similar between the two groups, suggesting that while NORSE survivors fare worse cognitively, the condition does not simply kill more patients.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that NORSE carries a distinct and severe burden of cognitive disability even among survivors, which has implications for how intensive care resources and rehabilitation planning are allocated for this patient group.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, retrospective. Small retrospective sample (N=81) from a single UK specialist centre limits generalisability; no long-term cognitive follow-up beyond discharge; cryptogenic NORSE (cause unknown) still accounts for half of cases, making prognosis inherently uncertain *Editor's fact-check note: Study covers two hospital sites (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery and UCL Hospital), so 'single-center' is slightly imprecise but both are within the same NHS trust and city; flagged as effectively single-institution. Sample sizes verified: total N=81, NORSE n=29, RSE n=52. Mortality figures verified: c-NORSE 20.0% vs etiology-identified NORSE 7.1%; overall NORSE 13.8% vs RSE 21.1% — direction of effect confirmed.*

studies.headline: Belgian doctors often don't recognise reproductive coercion when they see it
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a qualitative study with 18 French-speaking healthcare professionals in Belgium — mainly gynaecologists and general practitioners — to map their knowledge and perceptions of reproductive coercion, defined as behaviours that control a person's reproductive choices within an intimate relationship. The study suggests reproductive coercion exists in Belgium but remains a poorly understood and inconsistently handled issue in clinical practice.
studies.why_it_matters: If frontline clinicians cannot reliably recognise or respond to reproductive coercion, victims may pass through the healthcare system without receiving appropriate support — underscoring the case for structured professional training.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), qualitative only, single-center region (French-speaking Belgium), self-reported knowledge. Only 18 participants, all from French-speaking Belgium; findings may not generalise to other countries or healthcare systems. Qualitative design captures perceptions, not actual clinical behaviour *Editor's fact-check note: N=18 confirmed from abstract. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: Puerto Rican immigrants see their home culture as shaped by colonialism, not just tradition
studies.summary: Researchers used reflexive thematic analysis to explore how recent Puerto Rican immigrants (N = 19) living in Florida and Arizona described and evaluated Puerto Rican cultural values. Applying a critical consciousness framework, the researchers found that participants interpreted these latter values as products of colonial dynamics rather than intrinsic cultural traits.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings challenge the common practice in psychology of treating cultural values as static, essential characteristics of a group, suggesting instead that values like deference or dependency may reflect responses to systemic oppression. This has implications for how counsellors and psychologists approach Latine clients' identities and behaviours.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), qualitative/self-reported outcomes, single-center, observational design. Only 19 participants, all recent Puerto Rican immigrants in two US states — findings cannot be generalised to Latine communities broadly or even to all Puerto Ricans; qualitative themes reflect participants' own interpretations rather than measured psychological outcomes

studies.headline: AI ethics worries and screen fatigue are driving foreign-language learners to burnout, study in Chinese classrooms suggests
studies.summary: Researchers surveyed 545 university-level English-as-a-Foreign-Language (EFL) learners in China, testing whether technostress, digital fatigue, and concerns about AI ethics predict language-learning anxiety, digital burnout, and academic performance. Using structural equation modelling, the study found that all three digital stressors significantly increased foreign-language learning anxiety, which in turn fully mediated their effect on digital burnout. Technology self-efficacy moderated the relationship between burnout and performance, with international students benefiting more from high self-efficacy than domestic students.
studies.why_it_matters: As AI tools become embedded in education globally, this study suggests that unaddressed concerns about AI ethics and digital overload may compound learning anxiety in ways that undermine academic outcomes — a dynamic likely not confined to language classrooms.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, cross-sectional, single-center, sample limited to EFL learners in China. Cross-sectional survey design cannot establish causation; all measures are self-reported; the study is based in Chinese universities and the AI-ethics concerns students raised may reflect a specific regulatory and cultural context; findings may not generalise to Western educational settings

studies.headline: Where a childhood brain injury reaches — not just how big it is — predicts whether a child will walk and think normally years later
studies.summary: Japanese researchers retrospectively examined MRI scans from 25 children diagnosed with acute encephalopathy with biphasic seizures and late reduced diffusion (AESD) — a serious brain condition typically triggered by fever — at Tottori University between 1991 and 2022. They classified white-matter lesions by location and depth, then assessed neurological outcomes at least 12 months later. Lesions extending into deep white matter in the frontal and temporal lobes, and involvement of the thalamus and basal ganglia, were strongly associated with unfavorable outcomes; critically, damage in the region controlling movement (Rolandic area) was associated with motor paralysis even when only one side of the brain was affected.
studies.why_it_matters: The study suggests that early MRI lesion mapping in children with AESD could help clinicians identify which children face the greatest risk of lasting cognitive or physical disability, potentially guiding rehabilitation planning — though the small sample means findings are exploratory.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, retrospective, no adjustment for multiple comparisons. Extremely small sample (N=25) and no adjustment for multiple comparisons mean all findings are exploratory; single Japanese centre and a condition more prevalent in East Asian populations limit generalisability; retrospective design spanning three decades means imaging technology varied across cases *Editor's fact-check note: Authors themselves note in the abstract that the study is exploratory due to small sample size and lack of multiple-comparisons adjustment — both flagged in caveats. N=25 verified. Study conducted entirely in Japan (Tottori University), and AESD is a condition with notably higher reported prevalence in Japan; this geographic specificity is noted. Outcome split verified: 13 favorable, 12 unfavorable.*

studies.headline: Even the tiniest sense that your work will last is enough to motivate children — and adults
studies.summary: Four studies involving 604 children aged 4–9 and 582 adults tested how much a sense of significance — knowing that one's efforts will persist beyond the moment — affects motivation. Participants consistently preferred artistic activities where their work would be saved over activities that left no lasting trace, even when the significance was minimal. This preference drove children and adults alike to choose more effortful, productive tasks over easier ones, and simply enjoying the process did not fully make up for the absence of lasting significance.

studies.headline: Overactive amygdala in PTSD is driven by trauma itself, not genes — twin study confirms

Combat veterans with PTSD (n=10 pairs, 20 individuals) and combat veterans without PTSD (n=16 pairs, 32 individuals) each participated alongside their combat-unexposed identical twin. Veterans with PTSD showed heightened amygdala responsivity compared to their genetically identical, unexposed co-twins — confirming this is driven by the traumatic experience, not inherited biology — while unexposed co-twins of PTSD veterans showed reduced amygdala activation, suggesting a familial resilience factor.
studies.why_it_matters: By showing that an overactive amygdala in PTSD results from the trauma itself rather than pre-existing genetic vulnerability, the study bolsters the case that PTSD is an environmentally caused injury to the brain, which has implications for how the condition is understood and destigmatised.

studies.headline: Exercising more today is associated with going to bed on time weeks later — and self-control is the link
studies.summary: Researchers in China followed 385 undergraduate students (mean age 20.45; 54% female) across three monthly time points, measuring physical activity, self-control, and bedtime procrastination using a random intercept cross-lagged panel model that separates within-person change from stable personality differences. At the within-person level, increases in physical activity at Time 1 were associated with improved self-control at Time 2, which in turn predicted less bedtime procrastination at Time 3. The effect held after controlling for chronotype and perceived stress.
studies.why_it_matters: The study suggests that daytime exercise may help people stop doom-scrolling past bedtime not through willpower alone, but by replenishing the cognitive self-control resources that erode over the day — a potentially actionable insight for anyone struggling with sleep timing.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, study population limited to Chinese undergraduates, short follow-up (three months). All three key variables were self-reported; sample was exclusively Chinese university students, limiting generalisability; observational design precludes causal conclusions; follow-up was only three months with one-month intervals

studies.headline: Your emotional map of 'happy' and 'sad' may be arranged completely differently from everyone else's
studies.summary: Researchers developed and compared three methods for mapping how individuals mentally organise emotions — a multi-arrangement task (MAT), pairwise comparisons, and standard rating scales — in a within-subjects study of 103 participants. All three methods showed good test-retest reliability, but they differed markedly in how richly they captured individual differences: some participants used up to five dimensions to organise emotions in the MAT, compared with two or three in the rating-scale approach. The MAT was found to be particularly useful for measuring how finely individuals differentiate between emotions.
studies.why_it_matters: Standard emotion research and psychiatric assessment assume people experience emotions in broadly the same way, but these findings suggest individuals' inner emotional landscapes vary so much that personalised approaches to diagnosis and therapy may be warranted.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=103), single-center, lab-based tasks may not reflect everyday emotional experience. Study involved only 103 participants in a lab setting; tasks involved rating emotional words rather than real emotional experiences; findings are preliminary and the clinical applications proposed by the authors remain speculative

studies.headline: Oxygen dips during sleep make it harder to read other people's faces
studies.summary: Researchers recruited 55 Icelandic adults (47.3% male, mean age 46) and had them complete a facial emotion recognition task, then undergo three nights of home polysomnography. Severity of blood-oxygen drops during sleep — the 'hypoxic burden' of sleep apnea — was independently associated with slower and less accurate recognition of emotional faces, even after adjusting for age, gender, and depression. Better sleep efficiency and more REM sleep were linked to faster emotion recognition, suggesting sleep architecture shapes this key social skill.
studies.why_it_matters: The findings suggest that untreated sleep apnea may quietly erode people's ability to read emotions in everyday social interactions, a consequence rarely considered when assessing the cognitive costs of poor sleep.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, observational design. Small Icelandic sample (N=55), observational design so causality cannot be established, single-centre study; findings need replication in larger and more diverse populations before they can be generalised

studies.headline: How much dementia caregivers feel their strengths are recognised in therapy predicts how well they cope afterwards
studies.summary: Researchers examined whether 'resource activation' — therapists actively drawing on clients' existing strengths — during telephone-based cognitive-behavioural therapy predicted how well family caregivers of people with dementia used coping resources after treatment. Caregiver-rated (but not therapist-rated) resource activation was significantly associated with better post-therapy resource use, with early-session activation appearing especially important for well-being and social support outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: For the millions of people caring for relatives with dementia — a role associated with high rates of burnout and depression — this suggests that how much caregivers feel their strengths are being recognised early in therapy may be a key ingredient in whether treatment actually helps them cope.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes, single-center, secondary analysis. studies.headline: Lupus silently reshapes the brain's communication networks — and immune markers predict how badly
studies.summary: Researchers in China used multimodal MRI and neuropsychological testing to compare structural-functional brain network coupling in 63 female SLE patients and 68 healthy controls. They found that lupus patients showed reduced coupling between brain structure and function, particularly in the default mode and frontoparietal networks. Specific blood immune markers — including anti-RNP antibodies and antiphospholipid-related components — were associated with these network disruptions, and reduced coupling in the default mode network correlated with lower cognitive scores on the MMSE.
studies.why_it_matters: Lupus is not typically thought of as a brain disease, yet this study suggests immune dysregulation may directly map onto measurable changes in how brain networks communicate — offering a potential framework for understanding cognitive decline in autoimmune conditions.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, female participants only. All participants were female, limiting generalisability; small single-center sample (N=63 patients) in China; observational design cannot establish causation; cognitive measure (MMSE) is a broad screen, not a sensitive neuropsychological battery

studies.headline: In Turkish TV dramas, cheating partners are usually family members — not strangers
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a qualitative content analysis of 19 prime-time Turkish TV series broadcast on five major channels in 2022. They identified 39 distinct infidelity incidents across the series and found that 95% of shows depicted infidelity. Strikingly, 64% of those incidents involved family or kinship networks — such as brothers-in-law, cousins, or sisters-in-law — while only 5% involved complete strangers. Unlike Western dramas that tend to frame affairs as individual pursuits of desire, Turkish series emphasised infidelity's damage to family honour and collective trust.

studies.headline: People with disabilities are largely invisible in gambling harm research — and that's a problem
studies.summary: This commentary — not an empirical study — reviews existing gambling research and argues that disability has been systematically overlooked as a context shaping gambling behaviour, harm, and access to treatment. The authors contend that disability type matters and that lumping all disabilities together obscures important differences in how gambling harms manifest and how prevention and treatment services are (or aren't) accessible. studies.headline: When you pick a card, any card, you're probably just reaching for the one closest to your right hand
studies.summary: Researchers at the Universities of Plymouth and Essex recruited 137 participants to select one of four face-down playing cards in a classic magician's 'force' setup, while their eye movements were tracked. Despite spending more time looking at the two central cards, participants' gaze patterns did not predict which card they ultimately chose. More reflective thinkers and those who deliberated longer were no less susceptible to the bias. Instead, the overwhelming predictor was physical reach: participants favoured the card requiring the least motor effort, supporting what the authors call the 'reachability hypothesis' over attentional or cognitive heuristic explanations.

studies.caveats: single-center, single experiment, laboratory setting, restricted stimulus type (playing cards only). Single laboratory experiment with playing cards only; findings may not generalise to choices involving more meaningful or familiar options; all participants were in a single physical setup, limiting ecological validity *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states n=137 and that 52% chose the middle-right card. Summary accurately reflects that attentional bias did not predict card selection and that reachability was supported. No corrections needed.*

studies.headline: Autistic kids can rewire their brain's response to sensory overload — but it doesn't always feel better yet
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, and Allied Disciplines
studies.summary: Researchers used fMRI to examine whether cognitive reappraisal — thinking about a sensation objectively rather than emotionally — changes brain responses to unpleasant touch in autistic and typically developing children. Autistic children showed reduced activity in sensory brain regions during reappraisal, suggesting a real neural effect, but — unlike their typically developing peers — they did not report feeling less bothered by the sensation. Older autistic youth and those with more severe sensory over-responsivity showed distinct patterns of frontal brain engagement, suggesting the strategy's effectiveness may depend on age and individual sensory profile.

studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, short follow-up. Small sample (N=92 total, 47 autistic), single-center US study, no long-term follow-up, and subjective ratings were taken immediately after each stimulus so emotional learning over time was not measured

studies.headline: New fathers' jealousy of the baby-mother bond predicts how much mothers unconsciously push dads away
studies.summary: Researchers at Ohio State University followed 182 different-sex, dual-earner couples from late pregnancy through nine months postpartum, examining how jealousy of the partner-infant relationship related to maternal gatekeeping — behaviours that either encourage or restrict fathers' parenting involvement. Mothers and fathers each reported their own jealousy at three months postpartum; gatekeeping was measured both by self-report and by coding observed mother-father-infant interactions. Maternal jealousy at three months predicted an increase in observed gateclosing (restrictive) behaviours by nine months. Notably, paternal jealousy was associated with fathers perceiving greater maternal restriction and less encouragement, even though it did not predict changes in observed gatekeeping over time.
studies.why_it_matters: The study highlights that jealousy — an emotion rarely discussed in the context of new parenthood — may quietly shape how involved fathers are allowed to become, with effects that are visible in behaviour but not always conscious or self-reported. This points to emotional dynamics in couples as an underexplored target for supporting father involvement.
studies.caveats: observational design, self-reported outcomes (for jealousy and reported gatekeeping), restricted to different-sex dual-earner couples, US sample only, single-center. Sample restricted to different-sex, dual-earner US couples — findings may not apply to same-sex parents, single-income families, or other cultural contexts; jealousy was self-reported and may be subject to social desirability bias; observational design precludes causal conclusions *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract states N=182 couples and that maternal jealousy predicted increases in observed (not self-reported) gateclosing — a critical distinction accurately captured in the summary. Paternal jealousy finding (associated with perceptions but not observed change) also accurately represented.*

studies.headline: AI counsellors reduce anxiety faster than human therapists in unemployed adults
studies.summary: Researchers conducted a 6-month randomised longitudinal study comparing AI-delivered versus human-delivered structured counselling in 400 unemployed adults, assessing outcomes across 13 measurement waves. Both formats were associated with significant reductions in anxiety and gains in career adaptability. However, the AI-delivered condition was associated with steeper anxiety reductions and faster improvements in career adaptability than human counsellors — a difference seen in the rate of change rather than when improvements began.
studies.why_it_matters: As AI-based mental health tools proliferate, this study suggests that — at least within structured behavioural interventions — AI delivery may accelerate psychological improvement, raising important questions about how and why human connection affects the pace of therapeutic change.
studies.caveats: single-center, study population based in China/Southeast Asia (generalisability unclear), short follow-up (6 months), self-reported outcomes likely. Study was conducted in China and Malaysia — cultural attitudes to AI and counselling may differ significantly from Western contexts; outcomes were likely self-reported; the intervention was highly structured, so findings may not apply to open-ended or complex psychotherapy; six-month follow-up leaves long-term durability unknown *Editor's fact-check note: Abstract does not explicitly state self-reported outcomes but anxiety and career adaptability measures in this field are typically self-report; flagged as likely. studies.headline: Your THC blood test might flag you as impaired the morning after smoking — even when your driving is fine
studies.summary: Researchers at CAMH in Toronto tested 65 frequent cannabis users (≥4 times/week) on a driving simulator and cognitive tasks 12–15 hours after their last evening cannabis use. studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), observational design, single-center, self-reported cannabis use patterns. studies.headline: People who constantly compare their bodies to others are surprisingly immune to a technique designed to improve body image
studies.summary: Polish researchers tested whether evaluative conditioning — a learning technique that pairs neutral symbols with positive or negative images — could shift attitudes toward body-related cues in 146 adults. studies.why_it_matters: Evaluative conditioning is being explored as a potential tool for body image interventions, but this study suggests that the people most likely to engage in harmful body comparisons — arguably those most in need of help — may be the least responsive to this approach. This has implications for how such techniques might need to be tailored.
studies.caveats: small sample (N=146, borderline), single-center, laboratory task with artificial stimuli (geometric shapes), Poland-only sample, no clinical population. studies.headline: Trainee therapists don't consistently overestimate their skills — they misjudge in surprising directions
studies.summary: Researchers analysed data from 73 psychology students taking part in an RCT on clinical supervision, comparing students' self-assessments of their therapy skills with ratings from independent observers and supervisors. Students' communication skills, empathy, and therapeutic alliance were evaluated from multiple viewpoints using a truth-and-bias model. Contrary to the widely held assumption that trainee therapists overestimate themselves, no consistent pattern of overestimation emerged: students overestimated therapeutic alliance relative to observers but actually underestimated their own empathy relative to supervisors. Across all skills, self-assessments showed no significant accuracy when compared to external ratings.
studies.why_it_matters: Training programmes widely rely on self-reflection as a tool for therapist development, but if trainees' self-assessments are neither reliably biased nor reliably accurate, supervision and feedback structures may need rethinking.
studies.caveats: small sample (N<100), single-center, self-reported outcomes, secondary analysis. Small sample (N=73), secondary analysis of an existing RCT, single institution in Germany, and all ratings are subjective — the study cannot tell us whether more accurate self-assessment would actually produce better therapists

studies.headline: Your brain can't extract visual averages without paying attention first
studies.summary: Researchers tested whether the brain can statistically summarise groups of visual objects (ensemble perception) without directed attention, using a spatial cueing task with EEG in 30 young adults (mean age 19.6). studies.headline: A progesterone pill cuts cannabis cravings in women — but does nothing for men
studies.summary: Researchers at the Medical University of South Carolina ran a randomised, placebo-controlled trial in which 148 adults with cannabis use disorder (82 male, 66 female) took progesterone 200 mg twice daily or placebo for one week while abstaining from cannabis. At the end of treatment, participants underwent a laboratory stress task (Trier Social Stress Test) followed by a two-week medication-free follow-up. Progesterone reduced stress-induced cannabis craving in women but not men, and normalised the relationship between subjective stress and cortisol in women and between stress and craving in both sexes. Higher stress-induced cortisol responses were also associated with longer time to first cannabis use during follow-up across the whole sample.
studies.why_it_matters: Cannabis use disorder lacks approved pharmacotherapies, and stress-triggered relapse is a leading obstacle to recovery; these findings suggest that sex-hormone-based treatments could open a personalised medicine avenue specifically for women.
studies.caveats: short follow-up, single-center, non-treatment-seeking sample, industry funding [Achieve Life Sciences, Indivior, Jazz Pharmaceuticals, Aelis Farma, PleoPharma — disclosed by authors]. Only one week of treatment; participants were not seeking treatment (may not represent typical patients); single US centre; some authors have industry ties; follow-up was only two weeks, so long-term relapse prevention is unknown
